title: Coles investigates cyber-attack, says no data compromised and urges password updates
content:
Australia’s second‑largest retailer, Coles, announced on Monday that it is investigating a cyber‑attack targeting its systems. The company said the investigation is being conducted with assistance from the Australian Cyber Security Centre and global security experts. Coles stated that, to date, no customer, team or supplier data has been compromised, but it remains too early to determine whether any information has been stolen.

The retailer apologized to customers and advised them to update their passwords as a precaution while the probe continues.
summary: Australia’s second‑largest retailer Coles said it was targeted in a cyber‑attack and is investigating the threat with the Australian Cyber Security Centre and global security experts. The company said no customer, team or supplier data had been compromised and advised people to update their passwords as a precaution.

title: See Jupiter and Mars make a spectacular close approach overnight Nov. 15-16
content:
On the night of November 15-16, stargazers in the United States can observe a close approach between Jupiter and Mars in the constellation Leo. The two planets will rise over the eastern horizon around midnight, appearing slightly more than 1 degree apart. This alignment occurs as the blue-white light of the star Regulus glows below them. According to In-The-Sky, the pair will not be this close again until July 2029.

Although the planets appear side by side, they are actually separated by over 368 million miles (592 million kilometers). The light from Regulus has traveled approximately 79 light-years to reach Earth. This visual phenomenon, known as an appulse, happens once every 2 to 2.5 years when Mars catches up to Jupiter in its more distant orbit.

Both Mars and Jupiter are superior planets, meaning their orbits are beyond Earth’s. Consequently, they always appear as full disks through a telescope, unlike Mercury and Venus which show phases. A 6-inch telescope can reveal distinct features of each world. Jupiter displays cloud bands and zones formed by ammonia and water masses moving through its hydrogen and helium atmosphere via jet streams. Mars appears as a reddish, ochre disk with dark surface features where basaltic rock is exposed after iron-rich dust has been scoured away, according to NASA.
summary: Heads up stargazers! Mars meets Jupiter for a spectacular rendezvous in the heart of the constellation Leo on the night of Nov.

title: Apollo 12 Launches Nov. 14, 1969, Achieves Pinpoint Landing Near Surveyor 3
content:
On November 14, 1969, NASA launched the Apollo 12 mission, marking the second crewed landing on the moon. The crew consisted of commander Pete Conrad, lunar module pilot Alan Bean, and command module pilot Richard Gordon. While Gordon remained in the command module to orbit the moon, Conrad and Bean descended to the lunar surface. Unlike the previous Apollo 11 mission, which drifted from its planned landing zone, Apollo 12 achieved a pinpoint landing in the Ocean of Storms.

The primary scientific objective was to land near Surveyor 3, a robotic lander that had touched down on the moon more than two years prior. Scientists aimed to examine the spacecraft to assess its durability in the lunar environment. The Apollo 12 astronauts visited the lander and collected samples to return to Earth. Additionally, the crew gathered 75 pounds of moon rocks, most of which were basalts formed from molten lava. These samples indicated that the landing site was more than 3 billion years old.

The mission demonstrated that the Apollo program could consistently land in specific areas identified by geologists, proving that the Apollo 11 landing was not a one-off event. This capability was essential for future, more ambitious exploration. The launch also highlighted the importance of a well-prepared Mission Control team, which possessed detailed knowledge of the spacecraft’s systems. This expertise was critical for the program's success and would later prove vital during the Apollo 13 mission.
summary: Apollo 12 launched on Nov. 14, 1969, with commander Pete Conrad, pilot Alan Bean, and command module pilot Richard Gordon. The crew performed a pinpoint landing in the Ocean of Storms near Surveyor 3, collecting 75 pounds of basaltic moon rocks older than 3 billion years.

title: Rory McIlroy Dedicates Record-Equalling Eighth Race to Dubai Title to Father
content:
Rory McIlroy has claimed a record-equalling eighth Race to Dubai title, a victory he emotionally dedicated to his father, Gerry, who is currently recovering from major surgery in the United States. McIlroy was moved to tears while recalling a parting message from his father, who had urged him to “Go and win the Race to Dubai” before McIlroy traveled to the closing events of the DP World Tour season.

The Northern Irishman finished second in the DP World Tour Championship in Dubai, posting a final round of 67. This result was sufficient to secure the season-long order of merit crown, allowing him to edge out Eugenio Chacarra by a narrow margin of 125 points. While Tyrrell Hatton won the tournament itself, Chacarra’s third-place finish meant McIlroy prevails in the overall standings. McIlroy later revealed that his father had been at the forefront of his mind throughout the competition.
summary: Rory McIlroy won his eighth Race to Dubai title after finishing second at the DP World Tour Championship, edging Eugenio Chacarra by 125 points. He dedicated the victory to his father, Gerry, who is recovering from major surgery in the United States.

title: Terry Butcher reflects on Maradona's Hand of God goal
content:
Former England centre-back Terry Butcher recently answered questions from Guardian readers in a London office during the week he was presented with his England legacy cap. The session addressed topics including his interactions with Diego Maradona and manager Bobby Robson. Butcher recalled the 1986 World Cup quarter-final against Argentina, where he was notably affected by Maradona’s “Hand of God” goal.

Butcher detailed a specific post-match encounter at the Azteca stadium, where he and Maradona were together in the doping-control room. He described tapping his head and then his hand to reference the controversial goal. Maradona responded by tapping his head, but did not acknowledge the handball. Butcher noted that Maradona avoided admitting to the infraction because doing so would have validated Butcher’s accusation.
summary: Terry Butcher, former England centre‑back, talks about the 1986 World Cup match against Argentina and Maradona’s Hand of God goal. He recalls being in the post‑match doping‑control room and noting that Maradona did not admit to the goal.

title: Wales Seismic Victory Over All Blacks in Cardiff
content: Seismic victory in Cardiff was cathartic and though Steve Tandy urges caution, maybe the ‘Welsh problem’ can be fixed So that’s that fixed then. Wales are back and all is right with the world. Suddenly the dysfunction at the union, the financial plight, the disputes, the emptying stadiums, the defeats – oh, the defeats – feel a very long way away. The All Blacks have been beaten. Seventy-three years of hurt, no more need for dreaming. The euphoria in the Principality Stadium, however many people were there – or more pertinently not – seemed as eerily familiar as it was cathartic. This was how Cardiff used to feel on match day.
summary: Wales won a seismic victory over the All Blacks in Cardiff, with Steve Tandy urging caution. The win ended 73 years of hurt and brought euphoria to the Principality Stadium, signalling Wales are back.

title: England's Three Lions win over Spain in two acts: first superb, second heroic
content:
Sid Lowe describes England’s victory over Spain as a match played in two distinct acts, with the first being superb and the second heroic. In the final, tense moments, the world champions continued to press, while England’s hold on possession had significantly declined. During this period, Dan Burn was substituted on, and the scoreboard displayed a 4-0 lead, but the clock seemed to move slowly as Spain kept returning to the attack.

Harry Kane left the bench to stand beside manager Thomas Tuchel, using hand gestures to direct his teammates to hold onto their lead. Tuchel nudged Kane playfully before fourth official Marc Bollengier ordered the captain back to the bench. However, Kane soon rejoined his teammates, who were standing together awaiting the conclusion of the game.

From the sideline, Kane witnessed James Trafford make a double save, a heroic moment that allowed England to survive the pressure. He also saw Dan Burn clear a final header just before the referee blew the whistle. Following the final whistle, Kane and his teammates ran back onto the pitch to celebrate the win.
summary: England beat Spain in a final where Dan Burn scored the decisive goal. Harry Kane and Thomas Tuchel guided the team, and James Trafford made a double save to secure the victory.

content:

title: NFL roundup: Vikings win on Cousins’ return; Hutchinson reportedly ends season celebrating sack
content:
The Minnesota Vikings secured a 7‑2 victory over the Green Bay Packers, with Kirk Cousins leading the comeback after rejoining the team from the Las Vegas Raiders at the trade deadline. Cousins completed 21 of 31 passes for 207 yards and threw two touchdown passes in his first game back, five days after the move. Levi Drake Rodriguez contributed two of the Vikings’ eight sacks in the win.

Other NFL highlights included Detroit’s fifth consecutive victory in Munich, Patrick Mahomes throwing five touchdown passes in a Chiefs win, and the Buffalo Bills improving to an 8‑1 record following their win over the Jets.

Cousins’ return came after his last appearance at Lambeau Field, when he tore his Achilles tendon in a 24‑10 Minnesota victory on October 29, 2023. His performance has revitalized a Vikings offense that had stalled under former quarterbacks Kyler Murray and Carson Wentz.
summary: NFL roundup: Vikings win on Cousins’ return; Hutchinson reportedly ends season celebrating sack.

title: Mirra Andreeva wins WTA Finals at Indian Wells, defeats Elina Svitolina 7-5, 6-3
content:
Mirra Andreeva captured the WTA Finals at Indian Wells by defeating Elina Svitolina 7‑5, 6‑3. The 19‑year‑old Russian earned the world No. 2 ranking and completed the tournament without losing a set.  

During the first set, Andreeva served for the break at 5‑4 but began the game with two double faults and two unforced errors, allowing Svitolina to take the break.  She quickly recovered, won the next five games, and regained momentum to close out the set.  

After regaining the break, Andreeva continued her strong play, securing a second‑set win and her first WTA Finals title.
summary: Mirra Andreeva defeated Elina Svitolina 7-5, 6-3 to win the WTA Finals at Indian Wells for the first time. The victory earned her the world No 2 ranking and she dominated the tournament without losing a set.

title: England beat Spain after Anderson red to top Nations League group
content:
England secured first place in their Nations League group after a 3‑2 victory over Spain, a result that came on the back of a red card to England’s defender Anderson. The win was enough to top the group and move England ahead of Spain in the standings.

Spain entered the match with a remarkable record, having lost only once in 43 games—a penalty defeat to Portugal in last year’s Nations League final. Thomas Tuchel praised the team’s resilience, noting that Spain had “forgotten how to lose.” The match saw England hold off a spirited Spanish fightback, with the red card proving pivotal in maintaining the lead.

The scoreline echoed a historic encounter from 2018, when England beat Spain 3‑2 in Seville. That result is remembered as one of Sir Gareth Southgate’s most celebrated victories, and Tuchel felt the same excitement and confidence at the end of the recent game.
summary: England beat Spain after Anderson red to top Nations League group.

content: A new experiment using CRISPR gene‑editing delivered a single infusion to monkeys and maintained low triglyceride levels for three years. Researchers say the results demonstrate the potential to control blood fats through a lasting DNA change, which might eventually replace the need for daily drug doses.
summary: A single infusion of a gene‑editing treatment lowered triglyceride levels in monkeys for three years. The findings suggest a lasting DNA change could control blood fats and may replace daily medication.

title: Urban growth in São Paulo Metro Area collapses stream food webs, cutting connections
content:
Urban expansion in Brazil’s São Paulo Metropolitan Area is driving the collapse of food webs in local streams, according to a new study. The research links the advance of urbanization directly to severe ecological disruption in these waterways.

Published in August in the journal Nature Cities, the study finds that degradation does more than reduce species numbers; it selectively removes organisms according to size and streamlines ecological interactions. As a result, the complexity of stream networks falls dramatically, with connections dropping from 190 to just three.
summary: Urbanization in the São Paulo Metropolitan Area is causing the collapse of food webs in local streams. A study published in August in the journal Nature Cities found that degradation selectively eliminates organisms by size, simplifying ecological interactions and reducing network connections from 190 to three.

title: Milk and wine found in 2,000‑year‑old Menorcan funerary vessels
content:
Archaeologists have identified milk and wine as remnants of funerary rituals in Menorca dating to the Late Iron Age, or post-Talayotic period, over 2,000 years ago. During this era, the Balearic Islands experienced increased connectivity with the wider Mediterranean while maintaining local traditions, such as burying the dead in rock-cut tombs or artificial caves. These sites often featured external courtyards in front of burial chambers where animal offerings were likely made.

Researchers had previously suspected that perishable foods or liquids were offered in characteristic high-bottomed ceramic vessels, but the specific contents of these containers had never been identified until now. This discovery provides new insight into the distinct funerary practices of the region during a time of growing external contact.
summary: In the Late Iron Age, over 2,000 years ago, Menorca’s rock‑cut tombs contained ceramic containers. Analysis shows those containers held milk and wine, indicating perishable food and liquid offerings in island funerary rituals.

title: Drone survey finds stable and declining Erect‑crested penguin populations in NZ
content:
A drone survey of New Zealand’s endangered erect‑crested penguins has identified a stark contrast in population trends. One group has remained stable for decades, while another has fallen by more than 40 percent, a decline attributed to predators, worsening storms and changing ocean conditions.

The study also found that the tiny Bounty Islands host nearly as many breeding pairs as the much larger Antipodes Islands, even though the Bounty Islands are about 40 times smaller in area.
summary: A drone survey of New Zealand’s endangered Erect‑crested penguins shows one population has remained stable for decades while another has declined by more than 40%, linked to predators, worsening storms and changing ocean conditions. The tiny Bounty Islands support nearly as many breeding pairs as the Antipodes Islands despite being about 40 times smaller.

title: Physicists use laser flashes to align tiny electrical regions in crystal
content: Physicists have shown that brief flashes of laser light can arrange tiny electrical regions within a crystal, a technique that resolves a longstanding mystery about the material’s behavior. The laser‑induced alignment persists for only a trillionth of a second, but researchers say the finding may enable new methods for processing and storing information.
summary: Scientists discovered that flashes of laser light can organize tiny electrical regions inside a crystal, solving a decades‑old mystery about the material’s behavior. The laser‑induced alignment lasts just a trillionth of a second, but the breakthrough could open the door to new ways of processing and storing information.

title: Fossil teeth show dinosaurs ate seaweed over 100 million years ago
content: New research has identified chemical signatures in fossilized dinosaur teeth that point to the consumption of seaweed and other marine foods more than 100 million years ago. The analysis suggests coastal dinosaurs and other prehistoric animals incorporated nutrients originating from the sea into their diets. The study further indicates that marine resources moved through ancient food chains, providing supplemental nutrition to a range of species, from herbivorous dinosaurs to carnivorous predators.
summary: Researchers found chemical signatures in fossilized dinosaur teeth that indicate they consumed seaweed and other marine foods more than 100 million years ago. The evidence suggests coastal dinosaurs and other prehistoric animals incorporated marine nutrients into their diets, supplementing both herbivores and predators.

title: ESA's Euclid telescope finds 31 ancient quasars, two as bright as a trillion suns
content: ESA’s Euclid space telescope has identified 31 ancient quasars, including two that emitted light comparable to a trillion Suns when the Universe was roughly 670 million years old. Powered by supermassive black holes, these quasars illuminate a period when the first galaxies were still coalescing.
summary: ESA’s Euclid space telescope discovered 31 ancient quasars. Two of the quasars shone with the brightness of a trillion Suns when the Universe was just 670 million years old, powered by supermassive black holes and showing a time when the first galaxies were still taking shape.

title: Stripe closes small business account after $1,500 invoice, citing unauthorized payment risk
content:
A small business that connects homeowners with local contractors posted on Hacker News that its Stripe account was closed after a single $1,500 invoice was blocked. The company’s model bills contractors per appointment that actually occurs. After a recorded call in which a client agreed to the arrangement, the client saved his card through a $1 Stripe payment link, which was successfully processed. Weeks later the business invoiced the client for three completed appointments, charging the saved card for $1,500. Stripe blocked the payment and, two days later, terminated the account, stating that the payments “don’t appear to have been authorized by the customer.”

The business appealed through the Stripe Dashboard, submitting an appeal letter, company documents and the invoice. The appeal was rejected the next day as an “unacceptable level of risk.” Support replied that the business model “presents a level of risk we’re unable to support” and that the decision was final. After an internal escalation, Stripe sent a brief email reaffirming that it would not accept payments for the business. The company notes that Stripe never requested the call recording, the client’s messages, or direct confirmation from the client, who says he has not disputed the charge and will pay by bank transfer outside Stripe.

The poster asks whether anyone at Stripe can review the evidence, including a call with the client, and seeks advice from others who have faced similar issues on how to structure per‑appointment billing to avoid the appearance of unauthorized charges. The original Hacker News thread has attracted 108 points and 36 comments.
summary: We're a small business that sells pre-booked appointments with homeowners to local contractors, billed per appointment that actually happens. Our first client agreed to this on a recorded call and saved his card through a $1 Stripe payment link, which we planned to use for billing later.

content: A free application allows users to boot SteamOS within a virtual machine on Apple Silicon Macs. By running SteamOS this way, the Mac can access PC and legacy games that would not otherwise run on the hardware.

title: ULA Vulcan rocket fails 10 minutes after launch, destroying 40 Amazon Leo satellites
content:
United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket lifted off on 15 November 2026 carrying 40 Amazon Leo broadband satellites. The launch, conducted from Space Launch Complex 41, ended in failure when the vehicle experienced an anomaly about ten minutes after liftoff, according to a statement posted by ULA on X.

The mishap marks the first mission failure in ULA’s 20‑year operational history and prevented the delivery of the 40 Leo satellites to orbit. The launch was intended to be the first of 38 flights that Amazon has contracted with ULA. Leo, Amazon’s broadband satellite system and a competitor to SpaceX’s Starlink, has so far placed only a small portion of the satellites needed to challenge Starlink.
summary: ULA's Vulcan rocket lifted off on November 15, 2026 from Space Launch Complex 41 carrying 40 Amazon Leo broadband satellites. An anomaly occurred about 10 minutes into flight, marking ULA's first mission failure in its 20‑year history and destroying the satellites.

content:

title: ULA Vulcan rocket crashes minutes after liftoff, aborting Amazon satellite launch
content:
United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket, carrying 40 Amazon low‑Earth‑orbit broadband satellites, fell back to Earth minutes after liftoff on Sunday. The failure halted the mission that was intended to launch the first of 38 Vulcan flights Amazon has booked to expand its satellite internet network, which aims to compete with SpaceX’s Starlink.

The incident affects a vehicle that holds contracts to launch roughly half of the United States military’s national‑security space missions in the coming years. ULA officials indicated the rocket will remain grounded for an indefinite period while the cause is investigated.

Vulcan has previously experienced close calls, having encountered failures with its strap‑on solid rocket boosters on two of its four earlier flights. In those cases the rocket corrected the problems, completed orbit insertion, and subsequent months‑long reviews allowed the program to resume. Sunday’s mishap now adds another pause to the launch schedule.
summary: ULA Vulcan rocket crashes minutes after liftoff, aborting Amazon satellite launch.

The Iranian Revolutionary Guard explicitly claimed responsibility for both attacks.

The state‑run Bahrain news agency published statements from regional governments condemning the Iranian actions. Jordan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Qatar all issued strong condemnations and expressed solidarity with Bahrain.

It called for an immediate halt to the “blatant Iranian attacks” and urged serious steps toward security and stability in the region, warning that the escalation could undermine diplomatic efforts.

Bahrain’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs issued its strongest condemnation of the continued Iranian aggression, praising the efficiency, vigilance and capability of the Bahrain Defence Force for intercepting the drones and affirming the country’s readiness to deter any aggression. The ministry characterized the attacks as a resumption of Iran’s aggression that disregards international law and the UN Charter.

title: Comet 220P/McNaught brightens thousandsfold after gas-driven dust outburst
content:
Comet 220P/McNaught, discovered by Australian astronomer Robert McNaught in 2004, is a periodic comet that returns every five‑and‑a‑half years when it comes as close to the Sun as Mars. The comet is normally faint, with a brightness fainter than magnitude +15, and is usually beyond the reach of most amateur telescopes. This summer, however, the comet experienced two dramatic outbursts that made it visible to small telescopes and even to the naked eye in some cases.

The first outburst occurred on 14 June, as 220P approached perihelion at a distance of 1.5 astronomical units. On 31 May the comet was at magnitude +17.39, but within less than 14 hours it brightened to magnitude +11.05. By 2 June the brightness had increased further to magnitude +8.23, making it briefly visible in 10×50 binoculars from a dark site. The comet faded back to magnitude +12 by perihelion, but a second outburst began at the end of July. During that event the comet brightened from magnitude +14 on 28 July to magnitude 6.1 on 6 August.

The outbursts were caused by solar heating of the comet’s icy interior. As the Sun’s heat turned ice beneath the surface into gas, the escaping gas built up pressure and ripped the surface apart, ejecting huge amounts of dust into space. Models based on the observations indicate that between tens of billions and hundreds of billions of pounds of cometary dust were released. The dust, only a millionth of a meter across, expanded outward at about 1,280 feet (390 m) per second, scattering sunlight and creating a bright coma. Josep M. Trigo‑Rodríguez of the Institut de Ciències de l’Espai and the Institute of Space Studies of Catalonia stated that the comet detached localized parts of its crust, creating a dust‑rich envelope that increased the comet’s brightness by 250 times in half a day.

The 5.5‑year orbit places 220P in the Jupiter‑family of comets, which originate primarily from the Kuiper Belt and the Scattered Disk and later migrate inward. Studying outbursts such as those seen in 220P provides clues to the bulk characteristics of Jupiter‑family comets and informs research on impact hazards. After its close approach to Earth on 12 October at 1.04 astronomical units, the comet is now fading at magnitude +13. It will return to the inner solar system in late 2031, when it will again be observed by astronomers worldwide. The findings on 220P’s outbursts were published on 3 November in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society.
summary: Comet 220P/McNaught brightens thousandsfold after gas-driven dust outburst.

title: 300-foot Green Bank Telescope collapses on Nov. 15, 1988 in West Virginia
content: On Nov. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed. It happened at 9:46 p. M. On a clear night with no strong winds. When the observatory staff showed up to work the next morning, they were greeted by a huge pile of wreckage. The telescope collapsed under its own weight after a key structural element called a "gusset plate" failed. This was one of four connecting plates that held the telescope's large, metal beams together. Investigators found that these gusset plates were not built to last the 26 years that this telescope had been in use. Three years later, construction began on a new telescope. The Green Bank Telescope was even bigger and more sensitive, and it began science operations in 2001. (Image credit: NRAO/AUI/NSF) Why it mattered When the 300-foot telescope first debuted, it was not just the United States' largest radio observatory, but the largest such facility in the world. But its quick construction — just two years — led to it having to be significantly upgraded later. "In 1970, the 300-foot’s surface had become so warped from maintenance crews, snow, and its own weight that a new finer-meshed aluminum surface was installed," the website for the National Radio Astronomy Observatory reads. "A larger traveling feed was also installed at the prime focus." The collapse, however, was no one's fault. "Unforeseeable stress factors cracked a steel connector plate," wrote the NRAO. The Green Bank Telescope collapse left a mass of twisted debris behind. (Image credit: NRAO/AUI/NSF) During its years of observations, the 300-foot telescope contirbuted to the discovery of dark matter and the realization that pulsars come from supernova explosions. "One of the most important products to come out of the 300-foot telescope was an all-sky survey of radio objects called the Green Bank 6cm Survey. Nearly every northern hemisphere radio object studied by any other telescope is from a catalog compiled using this telescope," reads the NRAO website. Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube.
summary: On Nov. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed.

title: Space Jam's alien basketball match cited as a model for interplanetary dispute resolution
content:
The 1996 live‑action‑animation film Space Jam places the Looney Tunes in a crisis when a group of extraterrestrials called the Nerdlucks arrive on Earth. The Nerdlucks intend to abduct the cartoon characters and transport them to an outer‑space amusement park known as Moron Mountain. To avoid captivity, Bugs Bunny proposes a winner‑takes‑all basketball match between the Tunes and the alien visitors.

The Nerdlucks respond by using their technology to steal the basketball abilities of professional players, including Charles Barkley and Muggsy Bogues, transforming themselves into the intimidating Monstars. With the Tunes outmatched, Bugs and his friends enlist Michael Jordan—who had recently moved from basketball to baseball—to lead the Tune Squad in the decisive game. The film also features brief appearances by actor Bill Murray.

Space Jam frames the interplanetary conflict as a sports contest, contrasting it with other 1996 alien‑themed movies that rely on destroying the enemy’s spacecraft. The narrative suggests that a basketball game offers a fair arena where victory depends on teamwork rather than weaponry or technology. After the Tune Squad’s win, the Monstars turn against their commander, Mr. Swackhammer (voiced by Danny DeVito), sending him to the moon and subsequently befriending the Looney Tunes.

Director Joe Pytka, speaking to Entertainment Weekly, described Michael Jordan’s performance as professional, noting that Jordan “played himself” and that the film incorporated realistic references to his life. The movie’s resolution portrays the alien opponents as foot soldiers following orders rather than inherently evil foes, emphasizing humility and reconciliation after the contest.

Space Jam remains available for streaming on HBO Max, with subscription options that include a basic ad‑supported plan at $10.99 per month, a standard ad‑free plan at $18.49 per month, and a premium 4K plan at $22.99 per month.
summary: In the 1996 movie 'Space Jam', Bugs Bunny challenges the alien Nerdlucks—who become the Monstars—to a winner‑takes‑all basketball game to determine the Looney Tunes' fate. The piece argues that this plot offers a whimsical example of settling interplanetary disputes through sport.

title: Cheltenham November meeting hit by rain, fast ground and late track inspection
content: There is little the track’s bosses could have done to prevent the chaos on and off the track this weekend Even after two days of racing afflicted by dozens of non‑runners because of the fast ground, the elements still had not quite finished with Cheltenham on Sunday, when the third day of the track’s November meeting went ahead only after a late inspection – to assess standing water on the course after several hours of rain. A crowd of more than 10,000 racegoers, swelled by a big contingent of students from the specialist racing events organiser INVADES, had largely assembled when the inspection was announced, and while the course was passed fit for racing 15 minutes later, it was another uncomfortable moment for all concerned at the end of a tricky three days in the west country.
summary: Dozens of horses were withdrawn because of fast ground and heavy rain, creating chaos on and off the track during the three‑day meeting. After a late inspection for standing water, the course was declared fit 15 minutes later as more than 10,000 spectators, including many INVADES students, watched.

title: Tom Banton's 121 powers England to 135-run win over Australia in 2nd ODI
content:

The win came under lights on Sunday, with Tom Banton scoring a crisp 121 from 99 balls after England were asked to bat. Gus Atkinson also contributed as one of the architects of the emphatic total.

content:

content:

title: Turkey’s COP31 spotlight hides severe water shortage crisis
content:
Türkiye’s hosting of the 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) in Antalya has drawn global attention, yet the country’s most pressing concern is water scarcity. The Turkish team of the global climate‑advocacy group 350.org is led by Efe Baysal, who has been working with the government to align the summit’s agenda with national priorities.

Just weeks before the summit, wildfires erupted a few kilometres from the COP31 venue, burning 8,000 hectares of forest and injuring several people. The flames forced hundreds to flee their homes, underscoring how prolonged heatwaves and drought—conditions that are becoming more common in the region—create ideal conditions for fires to start and spread.

Türkiye’s climate crisis is evident in its record of extreme weather. In 2011 the country recorded more than 300 extreme events, a figure that rose to almost 1,500 by 2023, according to the Turkish State Meteorological Service. Drought is a particular threat to a semi‑arid nation, with half of the population projected to face water shortages by 2030. The last year saw the lowest rainfall in 61 years, and three‑quarters of Türkiye’s lakes have dried up over the past 50 years. Lake Iznik, the country’s fifth‑largest natural lake and the site of a fifth‑century Byzantine basilica, has retreated dramatically, exposing ruins that were once submerged.

Agriculture has felt the pinch as well. In 2025 crop and field production fell by 9 %, while fruits, beverage and spice plants lost nearly a third of their output. The agriculture ministry cited drought and frost as the main causes. Sinkholes, now numbering more than 1,000, are increasing in the Konya Basin, where groundwater levels drop about two metres a year due to reduced rainfall and excessive extraction.

Against this backdrop, Türkiye is pursuing a concrete energy transition. The COP31 presidency has launched the “35 by 35” electrification target, aiming for 35 % of final energy demand to come from electricity by 2035. The new National Energy Plan 2040 emphasises electrification and renewable‑energy expansion, but it still lacks a clear coal‑phase‑out timeline. A 350.org report notes that coal trade between Türkiye and Australia has produced roughly 75 million tonnes of carbon emissions since the Paris Agreement, and neither country has set a coal‑phase‑out date. In 2025 Türkiye surpassed its solar target, doubling its capacity in recent years, but the government must build on this progress to meet the summit’s climate‑action expectations.
summary: Efe Baysal leads the Türkiye team of global climate advocacy group 350. Org.

title: Sanaga‑Yong sanctuary in Cameroon cares for 75 rescued chimpanzees
content:
A rehabilitation centre in central Cameroon is providing a refuge for chimpanzees threatened by poaching, trafficking, insurgencies and traditional‑medicine practices. The Sanaga‑Yong sanctuary, founded in 1999 by primatologist Sheri Speede, serves as a haven for the region’s primates.

Each morning Speede begins caring for the sanctuary’s 75 chimpanzees, feeding them four times daily and checking them for physical or behavioural problems. More than 30 of the animals receive routine birth‑control medication, four infants require round‑the‑clock care, and two teenage chimpanzees are being introduced into new social groups.
summary: Primatologist and veterinarian Sheri Speede founded the Sanaga‑Yong sanctuary in 1999 to protect central African chimpanzees. title: Morton Salt mine in Ohio closes after underwater leak, threatens winter road safety
content:
A leak in a Morton Salt mine in Ohio has forced the company to close the facility permanently after water began gushing through a ceiling crack last month. The shutdown eliminates 77 local jobs in Fairport Harbor and its surroundings. Officials and residents are questioning the cause of the leak, the safety of nearby drinking‑water supplies, and how the region will obtain salt for de‑icing roads this winter.

The mine’s salt reserves have been a key source for keeping roads free of ice and snow across the wider area, and its closure raises concerns that a shortage could lead to travel disruptions during the winter season.
summary: Water gushed through a crack in the ceiling of a Morton Salt mine in Ohio, prompting the company to shut the mine down permanently. The closure eliminates 77 jobs in Fairport Harbor and raises concerns about drinking‑water safety and the region’s ability to source road‑salt for winter.

title: Indigenous students conduct wildlife survey retracing Lewis and Clark route
content: Two centuries after the expedition, Indigenous students are conducting a new wildlife survey along the route In 1804, when Thomas Jefferson dispatched Meriwether Lewis and William Clark and their Corps of Discovery to explore the newly acquired land west of the Mississippi, the president’s primary aim was political: Americans needed to establish presence, power and trade routes in these territories before the Europeans beat them to it. But Jefferson, an ardent naturalist, had a secondary agenda. He ordered that the expedition also survey the flora and fauna of these landscapes. On their two-year jaunt across the western half of the country, Lewis and Clark kept meticulous journals of the animals and plants they encountered: bison, horned lizards, sage grouse, prairie dogs, wild licorice and catfish, among them. These observations were pivotal in shaping an early understanding of North American biodiversity.
summary: Two centuries after the Lewis and Clark expedition, Indigenous students are conducting a wildlife survey along the historic route. Their work follows the original 1804 two‑year jaunt that recorded the region’s plants and animals.

title: Brain‑heart interactions studied in rats may forecast survival after cerebral anoxia
content:
Low oxygen levels in the brain, or cerebral anoxia, are a leading cause of death worldwide. Patients who recover from cerebral anoxia deal with persistent neurological issues that worsen their quality of life.

Building on previous work showing that brain–heart interactions can predict the severity of symptoms and survival, Diego Candia‑Rivera, Sofia Carrion‑Falgarona and colleagues from the Paris Brain Institute assessed whether brain–heart interactions in a rat model of severe oxygen loss can predict survival after resuscitation.

The work is published in eNeuro.
summary: Researchers at the Paris Brain Institute, including Diego Candia‑Rivera and Sofia Carrion‑Falgarona, used a rat model of severe cerebral anoxia to test whether brain‑heart interactions can predict survival after resuscitation. The study, published in eNeuro, builds on earlier work linking brain‑heart interactions to symptom severity and survival in patients with cerebral anoxia.

title: Schizophrenia-spectrum patients report fragmented time and altered sense of self
content: People with schizophrenia‑spectrum conditions often report a markedly altered sense of time and space. While most individuals notice that a minute can feel shorter when they are enjoying themselves and longer when they are bored or stressed, those with the condition may experience time as fragmented and their surroundings as strange or disconnected. Their perception of self can also shift, leading to a sense of personal disorientation that exceeds typical variations in time perception.
summary: Perceived duration of a minute varies, feeling shorter when having fun and longer when bored or stressed. People with schizophrenia-spectrum conditions often experience more extreme distortions, describing time as fragmented, familiar surroundings as strange or disconnected, and their sense of self as shifting.

title: Reanalysis finds no hidden black hole activity in galaxy UHZ1
content:
A recent study reexamining the galaxy UHZ1—previously dubbed an “outsize” black hole host—has questioned earlier claims of a massive, dust‑obscured black hole formed via direct collapse. Researchers reanalyzed existing X‑ray data and incorporated new infrared observations to probe the galaxy’s central activity.

Led by Fan Zou of the University of Michigan, the team found no evidence of hidden black hole activity. Their analysis, published in The Astrophysical Journal on Oct. 14, suggests UHZ1 is more likely a low‑mass, metal‑poor, star‑forming galaxy rather than a host of an unusually large black hole.
summary: A reanalysis of galaxy UHZ1 using existing X‑ray data and new infrared observations finds no signs of hidden black‑hole activity. title: International team finds giant prehistoric rodent fossils in southern Thailand
content:
An international team of paleontologists, including researchers from McGill University, discovered remarkably large rodent fossils in the pit of a mine in southern Thailand.

The finding, published in Scientific Reports, provides a new perspective on the early manifestation of rodent gigantism—the process by which animals evolve to become larger—demonstrating that the evolutionary history of large‑bodied rodents is considerably older and more geographically widespread than previously recognized, the researchers said.
summary: An international team of paleontologists, including researchers from McGill University, discovered remarkably large rodent fossils in the pit of a mine in southern Thailand. title: Study finds zero emissions commitment depends on amount of prior warming
content:
Global temperatures may keep rising even after human CO₂ emissions cease, a phenomenon described as the zero emissions commitment (ZEC). The ZEC refers to the temperature change that follows the complete halt of emissions and is often assumed to be close to zero.

A study led by the Met Office Hadley Centre, with co‑authors from several institutions including the University of Liverpool, found that the magnitude of the temperature response after emissions stop depends on how much warming has already occurred.
summary: Global temperatures may continue to rise after human CO₂ emissions stop, a change known as the zero emissions commitment (ZEC). Research led by the Met Office Hadley Center, with co-authors from institutions including the University of Liverpool, found the temperature response depends on how much warming has already occurred.

title: Tangled quantum vortices observed unraveling in ultracold Bose‑Einstein condensate
content: Researchers have observed tangled quantum whirlpools unraveling in an ultracold gas. When a cloud of atoms is cooled near absolute zero, it can form a Bose–Einstein condensate, a fluid in which all atoms share a single quantum state. Theory predicts that as a disordered quantum gas transitions to this ordered state, a tangle of tiny vortices forms and then gradually unravels, a process now captured experimentally.
summary: When a cloud of atoms is cooled close to absolute zero, the atoms can merge into a Bose–Einstein condensate, an exotic fluid where all atoms share a single quantum state. Current theories predict that as a disordered quantum gas settles into this ordered state, a tangle of tiny vortices forms and gradually unravels.

title: Lab experiments shed light on volcanic eruption‑triggered tsunamis
content: Tsunamis generated by volcanic eruptions remain poorly understood because the interaction of falling rocks and ash with seawater involves complex dynamics. This uncertainty hampers the ability to predict whether a volcanic flow will produce a tsunami and, if so, the potential size of the wave. Researchers have turned to laboratory experiments to investigate the mechanisms behind volcanic‑triggered tsunamis, but the extent to which these controlled models accurately replicate natural events is still unclear.
summary: Tsunamis triggered by volcanic eruptions are poorly understood because the dynamics of falling rocks and ash interacting with seawater are complex. Researchers have used laboratory experiments to study the process, though it is unclear how well the models represent reality.
author: Phys.org

title: Missouri study finds regular daily routines cut pain, depression in older adults
content: University of Missouri researchers report that older adults who maintain consistent daily schedules experience reduced physical pain and fewer depressive symptoms, even when they have insomnia. The study links regular timing of sleep, meals and other activities to better regulation of the body’s internal clock, which affects mood, sleep and overall health. The findings suggest that a simple adjustment to daily routines may improve both physical and mental well‑being for seniors.
summary: University of Missouri researchers found that older adults who kept consistent daily schedules reported less physical pain. The same group also reported fewer symptoms of depression even when they struggled with insomnia.
author: Science Daily

title: Rockefeller study finds arginine supplement boosts immunity against cancer, viruses
content: Rockefeller University researchers have reported that the amino acid arginine may bolster the immune system’s ability to combat cancer and viral infections. Their experiments showed that low levels of arginine impair immune recognition of harmful cells, while raising arginine intake reduced colon‑cancer tumor growth and improved outcomes of viral infections in mice. In a further test, mice given arginine after contracting influenza recovered more quickly, suggesting a potential therapeutic role for the supplement.
summary: Scientists at Rockefeller University found that low arginine levels impair immune recognition of dangerous cells, while higher arginine intake reduced colon cancer tumors and improved viral infection outcomes in mice. Administering arginine to mice after they contracted influenza also helped them recover.
author: Science Daily

title: Johns Hopkins study finds two brain regions shrink before memory loss in Alzheimer’s
content: Johns Hopkins scientists have identified early warning signs of Alzheimer’s disease that may emerge up to a decade before memory loss begins. Brain scans showed that two regions involved in memory and emotion begin to shrink before the hippocampus, the area doctors usually examine for Alzheimer’s indicators. The researchers linked these early structural changes to abnormal tau protein buildup, suggesting the shrinkage could serve as a new method for identifying individuals at risk for the disease.
summary: Johns Hopkins scientists found that warning signs of Alzheimer’s disease may appear up to a decade before memory loss begins. Brain scans showed two memory‑ and emotion‑related regions start shrinking before the hippocampus, a change linked to abnormal tau protein buildup that could help identify people at risk.
author: Science Daily

title: Astronomers discover dead star spinning every 8 minutes and sending radio pulses
content: Astronomers have identified a stellar pair located more than 5,000 light‑years from Earth in which a dead star spins once every eight minutes and emits mysterious radio pulses as it orbits a Sun‑like companion. The observations also show that the companion star experiences massive magnetic storms, providing new clues to an emerging astronomical mystery.
summary: Scientists have discovered a stellar pair more than 5,000 light‑years away where a dead star spins every eight minutes and produces mysterious radio pulses while orbiting a Sun‑like star. The observations also revealed massive magnetic storms on the companion star, providing fresh clues to an emerging astronomical mystery.
author: Science Daily

title: Simulations offer explanation for Uranus and Neptune's tilted magnetic fields
content: The magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune, noted for their extreme tilt, have long puzzled scientists since NASA’s Voyager 2 spacecraft examined the planets in the 1980s. Recent computer simulations propose that the unusual electrical properties generated by extreme conditions deep within these icy giants may account for those anomalous fields. The models further suggest that the planets’ magnetic poles could move by tens of degrees over only a few decades, a rate far faster than the pole shift observed on Earth.
summary: The strange, wildly tilted magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune have puzzled scientists since NASA's Voyager 2 spacecraft explored the planets in the 1980s. New simulations suggest that extreme conditions deep inside these icy giants create unusual electrical properties that could explain their magnetic fields.
author: Science Daily

title: NASA warns 2026 El Niño may exceed 1997‑98 monster event
content: NASA scientists say the rapidly intensifying 2026 El Niño may exceed the 1997‑98 event, which produced worldwide weather extremes. Satellite observations show striking similarities between the two patterns, suggesting the potential for major rainfall and flooding this winter, though the precise impacts are still uncertain.
summary: NASA scientists say the rapidly intensifying 2026 El Niño could surpass the historic 1997‑98 event. Satellite data show striking similarities and raise the possibility of major rainfall and flooding this winter, though exact impacts remain uncertain.
author: Science Daily

title: Vitamin C may block stomach cancer-linked chemicals, study suggests
content: Scientists report that vitamin C may inhibit the formation of potentially cancer‑causing chemicals in the stomach that arise after consuming nitrate‑ and nitrite‑rich foods. A newly developed mathematical model indicates that taking vitamin C after meals could lessen these reactions, suggesting a possible strategy for reducing cancer risk.
summary: Scientists have discovered that vitamin C may help prevent potentially cancer‑causing chemicals from forming in the stomach after eating foods containing nitrates and nitrites. A new mathematical model suggests that taking vitamin C after meals could reduce these harmful reactions, offering a possible new strategy for lowering cancer risk.
author: Science Daily

title: Gout affects 1.6 million UK adults and faces stigma despite rising cases
content:
About 1.6 million people in the United Kingdom are living with gout, a condition described as agonising yet often dismissed as a comical malady linked to over‑eating and inactivity. The prevailing perception can lead to stigma, prompting calls for ways to change attitudes toward sufferers.

The article illustrates the stigma through the experience of Brett McAllister‑Byrne, an urban planner in his early thirties. He first felt a sharp ache in his ankle and big toe the night after playing football, assuming it was a simple knock. The pain intensified, leaving him unable to work the following morning. When his family suggested gout, he expressed surprise, asking whether the disease could affect someone in their thirties.
summary: About 1.6 million people in the UK have gout, a condition increasingly common but often dismissed as a comical result of overconsumption and idleness. Urban planner Brett McAllister‑Byrne first felt sharp ankle and toe pain in his early 30s after football, missed work, and was surprised when his family suggested it might be gout.
author: Guardian Science

title: SpaceX Starship top section lands on Texas launch tower after 15th test flight
content: The upper stage of SpaceX’s Starship landed back on its Texas launch tower on Saturday, marking a milestone in the company’s work to qualify the vehicle for human spaceflight. The flight, the 15th test of the system, had been planned as a “double‑catch” mission in which both the upper stage and the lower booster would return intact. However, the booster experienced a malfunction, triggered an automated abort and exploded over the ocean, while the upper stage successfully returned to the pad.
summary: The top part of SpaceX’s megarocket Starship returned to its Texas launch tower on Saturday, marking a milestone for the company's human spaceflight efforts. The 15th test flight’s lower booster malfunctioned, triggering an automated abort and exploding over the ocean.
author: Guardian Science

title: SpaceX Starship returns to Texas launch tower after 22‑hour, 14‑orbit flight
content:
SpaceX’s megarocket Starship returned to its Texas launch tower on Saturday, marking a milestone in the company’s campaign to make the vehicle reusable. After a 22‑hour mission in which the craft completed 14 orbits of Earth, the 171‑foot (52‑meter) bullet‑shaped upper stage descended into the clutch of the tower’s mechanical arms and was caught for the first time.

Although the booster exploded, the successful capture of the upper stage demonstrates progress toward making Starship suitable for human spaceflight.
summary: SpaceX’s Starship returned to its Texas launch tower on Saturday, catching the 171‑ft upper stage in the tower’s mechanical arms for the first time despite the booster exploding. The flight lasted about 22 hours and the craft completed 14 orbits of Earth.
author: Guardian Science

title: SpaceX achieves first successful “chopstick” catch of Starship with Mechazilla tower
content:
SpaceX successfully captured Starship with its “Mechazilla” launch and catch tower for the first time, after aborting a planned catch of Starship Flight 15’s booster. The company had previously performed “chopstick” catches of its boosters, but this was the first successful maneuver on the Starship vehicle itself.

During the company’s third‑quarter earnings call, CEO Elon Musk noted that “success is not guaranteed on these first flights, but I'd say it's more likely than not that this succeeds next flight.” While the operation did not recover the entire launch vehicle, it marked a significant step toward reusable Starship launches.
summary: SpaceX captured the Starship vehicle using its Mechazilla launch and catch tower, marking the first successful “chopstick” catch of Starship after aborting a planned booster catch for Flight 15. The maneuver did not recover the entire launch vehicle.
author: The Verge

title: Jensen Huang Targeted in Chinese Spy Plot Reported by NYT
content:
The Stepback is a weekly newsletter that breaks down one essential story from the tech world. It covers Jensen Huang’s resignation and the fallout from Nvidia’s leadership crisis, and readers can follow Terrence O’Brien for more detail. The newsletter arrives in subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8 AM ET, and new readers can opt in through the provided link.

summary: This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on Jensen Huang's resignation and the fallout from Nvidia's leadership crisis, follow Terrence O'Brien.
author: The Verge

title: Sony's 1990s Aibo robot dog was designed as a family pet
content:
In the 1990s Sony anticipated a future where humanoid robots would become common in daily life, serving as coworkers, friends and even pets. The company developed the Aibo robot dog with the intention that it would join families as a pet.

The story of the Aibo is the focus of a recent episode of the podcast Version History. Host David Pierce is joined by The Verge’s Victoria Song and Jennifer Pattison Tuohy, and together they recount the robot’s origins and its notable success.
summary: In the 1990s Sony developed the Aibo robot dog as a pet meant to be part of the family. A Version History episode discusses the Aibo’s origins with David Pierce, Victoria Song and Jennifer Pattison Tuohy.
author: The Verge

title: LG B6E OLED TV 50% off at Best Buy this weekend
content:
LG has slashed the price of its B6E OLED television as part of Best Buy’s latest door‑buster event. The 55‑inch model is now 50 percent off, selling for $699.99 (a $700 discount) through the end of today, November 15. Larger 4K options are also discounted: the 65‑inch unit is $999.99 (a $900 discount) and the 77‑inch model is $1,499.99 (a $1,200 discount). These prices bring the B6E to an all‑time low, making it one of the most affordable OLED TVs available.

The B6E delivers the deep blacks and high contrast that OLEDs are known for, though it is not as bright as LG’s pricier C6 series. It comes with a simpler remote that does not include motion controls or voice features found on LG’s Magic Remote. The television supports Dolby Vision and HDR10 for lifelike colors, Dolby Atmos for immersive audio, and built‑in Apple AirPlay and Google Cast for easy streaming from mobile devices. LG’s webOS platform provides access to popular streaming apps such as Netflix, HBO Max, and YouTube.

Gamers will appreciate the 120‑Hz refresh rate, which is fast enough for modern consoles, and the TV’s variable refresh rate support—including Nvidia G‑Sync and AMD FreeSync Premium—to reduce screen tearing. The B6E is powered by an Alpha 8 Gen 3 AI processor and includes four HDMI 2.1 ports, allowing multiple console connections. While it lacks some of the advanced features of LG’s premium OLED models, the 50 percent discount makes the B6E a compelling choice for those seeking OLED performance at a lower price point.
summary: LG’s B6E OLED TV is discounted 50 percent at Best Buy, with the 55‑inch model priced at $699.99. The TV supports 4K, Dolby Vision, HDR10, Dolby Atmos, 120Hz refresh, and variable refresh rate with Nvidia G‑Sync and AMD FreeSync Premium.
author: The Verge

title: Rachelle Hampton won’t admit length of charting 'murmur' in Twilight
content:
Rachelle Hampton is a writer and co‑owner at Defector Media and the host of the Normal Gossip podcast, which presents anonymous listener‑submitted stories about everyday drama—from a lie about luxury wool in a knitting circle to an HOA president’s impeachment and a COVID outbreak at a destination wedding with 25 bridesmaids.  

The title notes that Hampton will not reveal how long she spent charting the use of the word “murmur” in the film Twilight. After years co‑hosting Slate’s In Case You Missed It, a podcast that kept her chronically online, she says she is now enjoying being a little more unplugged.
summary: Rachelle Hampton won’t admit length of charting 'murmur' in Twilight.
author: The Verge

title: Apple to unveil first non‑AR smart glasses at next June WWDC, shipments before year‑end
content:
Apple has confirmed that its first pair of smart glasses, the N50 prototypes, are reportedly “slightly thinner” than Meta’s second‑generation Ray‑Ban glasses. The devices are still a closely guarded secret, but Bloomberg analyst Mark Gurman said Apple plans to reveal the model at next year’s June WWDC. Gurman also noted that the glasses would not ship immediately, with shipments expected to begin before the end of the year.

The N50 glasses will not include augmented‑reality features. Instead, Apple is focusing on a revamped Siri AI that offers fine‑grained control over apps. By integrating these capabilities now and allowing iPhone developers to add support first, Apple hopes the glasses will be ready for immediate use once they launch.
summary: Apple’s first smart‑glass model, dubbed N50, will lack augmented‑reality features and is expected to be announced at June’s WWDC next year. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman says shipments could start before the end of the year and the glasses are slightly thinner than Meta’s second‑generation Ray‑Ban glasses, with a revamped Siri AI providing fine‑grained app control.
author: The Verge

title: Congress seeks stricter AI chip export rules after Nvidia spy scandal
content:
Congress is moving to tighten export rules on artificial‑intelligence chips following a scandal involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese spy. Lawmakers from both parties have expressed support for bills that would restrict such exports and have called for Huang and other Nvidia executives to testify before Congress.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said Huang and the Trump administration must answer to Congress, while Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott has sent letters to Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick requesting public testimony.
summary: Congress is moving to tighten export restrictions on AI chips after a scandal involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese spy. Democrats and Republicans, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott, have demanded that Huang, other Nvidia leaders and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick testify before Congress.
author: The Verge

title: South African winemakers turn to conservation as climate stress threatens vineyards
content:
More than 500 vineyards are spread across the slopes and valleys of South Africa’s Western Cape, a region that accounts for roughly 90 percent of the country’s wine production. Winemakers there are facing increasing challenges from drought, excessive heat and erratic rainfall, with temperatures rising 1.5 to 2 times faster than the global average over the past five decades and extreme storms becoming more intense as climate variability grows.

The late 2010s brought three consecutive years of severe drought, placing intense stress on vineyards and reducing grape yields. In response to the mounting pressure on grape production, many wine producers are expanding sustainability measures that have long been part of vineyard management. These steps reflect a growing focus on conservation practices within the industry.
summary: More than 500 vineyards in South Africa’s Western Cape, which supplies about 90% of the nation’s wine, are confronting drought, excessive heat and erratic rainfall. Many producers are expanding long‑standing sustainability practices, seeing conservation as a way to protect their business as climate pressures increase.
author: Ars Technica

title: James Webb finds ice older than Beta Pictoris star
content:
The James Webb Space Telescope has detected both water and carbon‑dioxide ice in the debris disk surrounding Beta Pictoris, a young star about 20 million years old and 64 light‑years from Earth. A research team led by astronomer Sarah Betti of the Space Telescope Science Institute used JWST to search the disk, which is known to contain a vast ring of dust and rubble where three planets are already confirmed.

The ice observed is glassy water ice, not crystalline, and it is mixed with carbon‑dioxide ice in roughly the same proportions found in comets of our Solar System. The findings imply that the raw materials needed to build water‑rich worlds may be common around young stars. Beta Pictoris, one of the most studied stars, has an edge‑on debris disk first imaged in 1984, where dust is continuously regenerated by collisions among comets and planetesimals.
summary: The James Webb Space Telescope observed the edge‑on debris disk around the 20‑million‑year‑old star Beta Pictoris, located about 64 light‑years from Earth. Researchers detected glassy water ice mixed with carbon‑dioxide ice that appears older than the star and matches comet‑like proportions, suggesting water‑rich planet ingredients may be common around young stars.
author: Ars Technica

title: SpaceX lands Starship on launch tower Saturday after horizontal flight
content:
SpaceX’s Starship vehicle returned to its launch site at Starbase in Texas on Saturday. After descending from altitude and emerging from a cloud deck, the spacecraft flew horizontally until three Raptor engines ignited, pulling it into a vertical orientation. The upper stage then moved slowly toward the launch tower, where two arms extended to receive it.

The tower’s arms featured two one‑foot‑wide nubs that provided the only points of contact for the vehicle. Within a minute of the ship becoming visible, the upper stage was captured by the tower’s arms, completing the recovery. SpaceX described the maneuver as a significant step toward developing and optimizing a large, rapidly reusable rocket.
summary: STARBASE, Texas —The black and silver ship fell out of the sky, emerging from the cloud deck near the very end of its flight. Incongruously, the rocket flew horizontal until the last moment when three Raptor rocket engines ignited and it swooped into a vertical position.
author: Ars Technica

title: Study finds 2020 COVID lockdowns reduced global average wildfire activity
content:
Wildfires affect regions across the globe and can pose serious threats to lives, as illustrated by the massive bushfires that swept southeastern Australia from 2019 to 2020 and destroyed thousands of homes, and the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires that spread widely across the city, causing extensive damage to local communities. While many causes contribute to wildfire ignition, humans are the sole factor capable of implementing preventative measures, though assessing their overall impact is complicated by the interplay of natural and human influences.

A research team led by Jianghao Wang, a professor at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, examined this issue in a study published in Cell Reports Sustainability. By comparing fire activity during the COVID‑19 lockdown period of 2020 with other years, the authors found that reduced human activity during the lockdowns corresponded with a net decrease in average fire activity.
summary: A team led by Jianghao Wang of the Chinese Academy of Sciences published a study in Cell Reports Sustainability comparing fire activity during the COVID‑19 era with other years. The authors report that reduced human activity during 2020 lockdowns lowered average global wildfire activity.
author: Ars Technica

title: Nvidia security chief left in August as CEO Jensen Huang steps down
content: Nvidia’s security chief departed quietly in August. The company’s CEO, Jensen Huang, has since stepped down, citing his relationships, including one with an executive at a firm suspected of funneling chips to China. A former intelligence officer described the incident as a leak that spreads through everyday conversation, noting that most corporate security teams lack the capacity to detect such breaches.
summary: Nvidia’s security chief quietly left in August. CEO Jensen Huang has stepped down over his relationships, including one with an executive at a company suspected of funneling chips to China, and a former intelligence officer said the leak reflects everyday conversations that most corporate security teams are poorly equipped to catch.
author: TechCrunch

title: TechCrunch's top gadget picks for Black Friday holiday shopping
content: TechCrunch reports that its team has reviewed numerous new gadgets this year and identified clear favorites to recommend for Black Friday shopping and the holiday season thereafter. The outlet’s selections are presented as enthusiastic product recommendations for consumers.
summary: TechCrunch's top gadget picks for Black Friday holiday shopping.

title: Grand Theft Auto VI: 10‑Year Development, Thousands of Staff, $1 Billion Cost
content: The latest instalment of the epic crime saga is finally here. We visit Rockstar Games for a hands-on encounter with the cultural event of the decade – and can confirm it more than lives up to the hype It still comes as a surprise for many to learn that Grand Theft Auto, the brazenly American crime series that has been one of the world’s most popular and most controversial video games for the past 20 years, is mainly made in Scotland. But if you grow up in Edinburgh, developer Rockstar North is part of the background mythology of the place. Plenty of people passed through this studio at some point or another in the 2000s, as game testers or employees. As a student in Edinburgh at that time, I would hear rumours of wild parties at the executives’ houses, as decadent as those in the game. At a bar or a birthday or a housewarming, you might meet a guy who claimed to have come up with one of the puerile puns that grace the in-game businesses (eg Nutsaki, a Japanese restaurant, or the fried-chicken chain Cluckin’ Bell). Grand Theft Auto is now made by a huge team of nearly 5,000 people around the world but its central nervous system is still in Holyrood, in the shadow of Arthur’s Seat. The setting of the latest Grand Theft Auto game really could not be further from the Scottish capital. Grand Theft Auto VI takes us to Vice City in the state of Leonida, a parody of Miami, Florida. It is a neon-soaked metropolis of sleaze and struggle, hard-partying excess juxtaposed with a barely concealed criminal underworld and unpredictable Florida madness.
summary: The game’s development spanned ten years, cost about a billion dollars, and involves nearly 5,000 staff worldwide. Although set in a fictional Miami‑like Vice City, its core development remains based at Rockstar North in Edinburgh, Scotland.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Headlines claim GTA VI release could trigger “GTA Flu” pandemic on Nov 19
content: Headlines have claimed the release of the first new GTA game in 13 years will hugely affect the global economy on Thursday – but there’s another story that’s been left behind A new pandemic is threatening planet Earth. It’s scheduled to hit 19 November. Entire offices and worksites will be emptied; employees struck down by a mysterious illness. But you need not panic: it isn’t fatal. It should pass in a few days. The anticipation for Grand Theft Auto VI, the first new game in the franchise in 13 years, is so high that a steady stream of news coverage has suggested it heralds economic catastrophe due to workers taking time off to play the game. The term “GTA Flu” was coined for the swathe of sickies that reportedly happened when GTA V was released in 2013, and – supposedly – are set to happen again when GTA VI comes out this week.
summary: Headlines have claimed the release of the first new GTA game in 13 years will hugely affect the global economy on Thursday – but there’s another story that’s been left behind A new pandemic is threatening planet Earth. It’s scheduled to hit 19 November.
author: Guardian Technology

content: Shatterproof wine glasses, Jellycat plushies, ‘yoga paws’ and more delightful gifts handpicked by our experts The best personalized gift ideas Nothing says holiday cheer quite like panic-browsing websites in pursuit of the perfect gift, toggling between 47 open tabs, eyes straining against your screen’s harsh blue light. summary: Guardian US curated a list of 143 holiday gifts for 2026 across kitchen, home, tech and other categories. Writers, shopping experts, their families, cats, dogs and kids tested the items to ensure they work for recipients.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Captcha scam uses key‑press test to install malware on users’ computers
content:
A new scam targets shoppers who visit small‑business websites during the holiday season. Instead of the usual image‑based or text‑based Captcha, the site presents a prompt that asks users to press a series of keys and then hit Enter to prove they are human.  

Security experts warn that this key‑press challenge is a vector for fraudsters to install malicious software on the visitor’s computer. The tactic exploits the trust users place in legitimate online stores and can compromise devices without the user’s knowledge.
summary: The scam replaces typical image or text Captcha with a prompt to press a series of keys and then press enter. Fraudsters use this interaction to install malicious software on the victim’s computer.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Italy fines Meta €805 million for accessing Android users' photos without consent
content: The fine is among the largest an Italian authority has imposed on a tech giant and Meta says it plans to appeal the decision Italy’s data protection agency has fined Facebook parent company Meta €805m ($887m) for accessing users’ photos without their specific consent. Through the Facebook application for Android devices, Meta accessed photographs, videos and related metadata belonging to Italian users “without obtaining specific consent and without properly informing them”, the authority said in a statement.
summary: Italy’s data protection agency fined Meta €805 million (about $887 million) for accessing photographs, videos and related metadata of Android users without specific consent. Meta said it will appeal the decision.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns amid spy-linked affair allegations
content:
Nvidia founder and chief executive Jensen Huang announced his resignation on Thursday, ending a 33‑year tenure at the company. In a letter to employees released over the weekend, Huang acknowledged that he had been unfaithful to his wife of 41 years.

The resignation follows a New York Times report linking Huang to a woman whom U.S. officials suspect of spying for the Chinese government. Media coverage also mentions allegations of two further affairs involving Nvidia employees. After the news broke, Nvidia’s share price fell sharply.

The developments have been described as a major corporate scandal, highlighting concerns about espionage activity within the U.S. technology sector.
summary: Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of Nvidia, resigned after 33 years following reports of an affair with a woman US officials suspect of spying for China. He admitted infidelity to his wife of 41 years and reports of two additional affairs with Nvidia employees, causing the company's stock to plummet.
author: Guardian Technology

title: SpaceX's Starship captured midair by tower arms in Texas after 22‑hour flight
content: SpaceX’s Starship spacecraft completed a 22‑hour flight and was caught midair by the giant mechanical arms at the company’s Texas launch tower. This event marks the first successful midair capture of a Starship returning from space.
summary: SpaceX's Starship spacecraft was caught by giant mechanical arms at its Texas launch tower after a 22‑hour journey. It was the first successful midair capture of a Starship returning from space.
author: Euronews

title: Space object 1998 KY26, 11‑metre body near Earth shows unexplained motion
content: The object designated 1998 KY26, about 11 metres wide, is moving near Earth, and its trajectory appears to be affected by forces other than the Sun’s or Earth’s gravity. This unusual behavior has led to speculation that it could be a Soviet probe missing for 40 years.
summary: The object known as 1998 KY26 is about 11 metres wide and is moving near Earth. Observations indicate that forces other than the Sun’s or Earth’s gravity are affecting its path and speed.
author: Euronews

title: Australia and Philippines sign defence pact amid South China Sea tensions
content: Australia and the Philippines have signed a new defence pact as tensions with China persist in the South China Sea. The agreement expands the Philippines’ growing military cooperation with Australia, Japan and the United States, encompassing joint exercises, the sharing of surveillance equipment and tighter coordination of their forces.
summary: Australia and the Philippines have signed a new defence pact. The agreement, part of the Philippines' effort to deepen military ties with Australia, Japan and the United States, includes joint exercises, surveillance equipment and closer coordination as tensions with China continue in the South China Sea.
author: Euronews

title: London’s Santa School trains professional Santas for 2026 Christmas
content: London’s “Santa School” is preparing professional Father Christmas performers for the 2026 holiday season. Participants are receiving instruction in sign language, updating their knowledge of current toy trends and practicing responses to the tough questions children may pose at Christmas.
summary: Father Christmas is heading back to a school in London where professional Santas receive training. The training includes sign language, updates on toy trends, and preparation for difficult questions children might ask.
author: Euronews

title: Canary Islands receive nearly 2,200 migrants in 48 hours, locals urge action
content: Spain reports that nearly 2,200 migrants arrived by boat in the Canary Islands over the weekend. The islands remain a key entry point into Europe for migrants from Africa. According to the Spanish Interior Ministry, more than 13,000 migrants have reached the islands between January and the end of last month. The information was provided by Andrew Hilliar, FRANCE 24 international affairs editor.
summary: Spain says nearly 2,200 migrants arrived by boat to the Canary Islands this weekend. The Spanish Interior Ministry says more than 13,000 migrants arrived there between January and the end of last month.
author: France 24

title: Record number of Democratic women elected to Congress and governorships in 2026 midterms
content:
Following the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, Gavin Lee welcomed Politico Senior National Politics Reporter Lauren Fedor. The exchange focused on the election outcomes that saw a record number of women elected to Congress and governorships across the country.

Fedor highlighted the growing presence of Democratic women in both chambers, noting that many of the new office‑holders are mothers of young children. She explained that voters across the map realized that moms were perhaps the best messengers for addressing concerns about the cost of living, affordability and how to make ends meet.
summary: Following the 2026 US midterm elections, a record number of Democratic women, many of whom are mothers of young children, were elected to Congress and governorships. Politico senior national politics reporter Lauren Fedor said voters viewed mothers as effective messengers on cost‑of‑living concerns.

title: Sheherazaad: Khudgarzi review | Ammar Kalia's global album of the month
content: (Erased Tapes) Dreamy, reverb-laden arrangements, virtuosic vocals and echoes of PJ Harvey and Massive Attack make this disarming debut a one-of-a-kind creation Since the release of her debut EP, Qasr, in 2024, south Asian-American vocalist and composer Sheherazaad has developed a distinctive take on the classical singing of her heritage. While her contemporaries such as the singers Ganavya and Manizeh draw on spiritual vocal traditions, and Arooj Aftab on jazz and folk instrumentation, Sheherazaad’s work is darker and far more introspective, using sparse acoustic arrangements to create a style of Urdu-language noir. On this debut album, she delivers her most disarmingly eerie and mournful work yet. A heavy layer of reverb coats the record’s spare and often evocative arrangements, making undulating tabla hits echo beneath Sheherazaad’s keening vocals on Qatil, while on Registaan it lends an unnervingly distorted quality to a simple guitar refrain and on Mard it subsumes melody in a haze of resonance. The resulting atmosphere sits somewhere between PJ Harvey’s late-90s eerie grunge and the trip-hop qawwali of Massive Attack’s work with singer Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan – an ambience that is as unsettlingly gloomy as it is engaging.
summary: Sheherazaad's debut album Khudgarzi features dreamy, reverb-laden arrangements and virtuosic vocals that draw comparisons to PJ Harvey and Massive Attack. The south Asian-American vocalist creates a darker, introspective style of Urdu-language noir using sparse acoustic arrangements.
