title: Charlotte Adigéry and Bolis Pupul Tour Their Home City of Ghent
content:
Art-pop duo Charlotte Adigéry and Bolis Pupul recently hosted a tour of their home city of Ghent, where they highlighted the Mammelokker, an 18th-century Flemish relief situated atop a grey gothic building in the town square. The stone sculpture depicts a daughter suckling her own father, a detail that aligns with the duo’s recent focus on blending pop and politics. Following their debut album, the Belgian artists are now processing their personal lives through their music.

The tour took place in late September under unseasonably warm weather. During the visit, Tom Zeebroek, one of the bandmates, encouraged visitors to look up at the Mammelokker, describing it as a gruesome architectural decoration. This stop was part of a broader itinerary through the medieval city, reflecting the duo’s goofy and spiky artistic sensibility.

title: Sainsbury Centre opens broad double-hander exploring love and heartbreak
content: Sainsbury Museum and Art Centre, Norwich With some uplifting works despite a certain obviousness, this broad double-hander tackles the vast topics of love, smooching and the aftermath To quote 1980s soft rockers Foreigner, I want to know what love is. And I want the Sainsbury Centre to show me. This big winter series tackles love in all its guises – and for now comprises two shows, one about smooching called The Last Human Kiss, another about desire and heartbreak called Ecstasy and the Aftermath. The problem is, love is probably the biggest topic in human history, let alone art history. Think of the endless novels and poems and films; think of how many songs have been written, how many paintings painted. Love is an endlessly vast topic and this show barely scratches its surface.
summary: The Sainsbury Centre in Norwich has launched a winter series comprising two exhibitions, The Last Human Kiss and Ecstasy and the Aftermath. The review notes that while the shows offer uplifting works, they only barely scratch the surface of the vast topic of love.

content:

Transportation officials cited “extraordinary circumstances” caused by communications issues at regional air traffic control centers for the stoppage.

Some teams searched for hotel rooms, while others rescheduled flights and leagues adjusted start times. title: Scientists find blood biomarker for diagnosing CTE in living patients
content:
Scientists have identified a blood biomarker that detects an advanced form of chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a degenerative brain condition caused by repeated head trauma. This discovery moves the medical community closer to diagnosing CTE in living patients. Currently, the condition can only be confirmed posthumously through the examination of brain tissue.

CTE is particularly prevalent in collision and contact sports, including American football, rugby, and football. Researchers express optimism that this breakthrough represents a significant step forward in the diagnostic process for the disease.
summary: A study identified a blood biomarker that detects an advanced form of chronic traumatic encephalopathy, moving closer to diagnosing the condition in living people. Currently, CTE, which is prevalent in collision sports, can only be diagnosed after death by examining brain tissue.

These workers, hired as the day’s production crew, were accustomed to heavy logging machinery rather than the sounds of adult filming. They transported a small group of humans in animal suits, known as furries, through the forest, taking care to prevent tails from dragging in the mud.

Once the furries were positioned, the director closed the set to allow the filming of a private group sex scene. Kaechele commented on the participants, describing them as adorable and noting that their adult acts appeared cute and innocuous.
summary: Kirsha Kaechele, the ‘first lady’ of Hobart’s Museum of Old and New Art, has launched an OnlyFans portal with the goal of helping preserve Tasmania’s rainforests. The launch featured a controversial production with furries and a private group sex scene that Kaechele described as adorable and innocuous.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Music festivals promote sustainability with compostable cutlery and charter buses
content:
As warmer weather marks the peak of Australia’s outdoor music and festival season, organizers are promoting sustainable travel options to reduce environmental impact. The Strawberry Fields festival, a multi-day music, arts, and wellbeing event located on the banks of the Murray River near Tocumwal in New South Wales, is positioned as a key example of these efforts. Although the site is a three-hour drive from Melbourne and seven hours from Sydney, the majority of fans are expected to avoid using private vehicles.

Instead of 16,500 attendees arriving by car, participants can utilize more than 118 charter buses operating across New South Wales and Victoria. Alternatively, they may travel via a combination of public transport and shuttle services. These initiatives align with broader sustainability goals, as highlighted by the "Change by degrees" series, which provides tips for reducing household carbon footprints and encourages readers to share their own emission-reduction strategies.
summary: The Strawberry Fields festival near Tocumwal offers over 118 charter buses to reduce private vehicle use. Attendees are encouraged to compost their cutlery to avoid environmental damage at campsites.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Norfolk storms fell trees, leaving some standing due to spalting
content:
In Caistor St Edmund, Norfolk, recent storms have left a woodland floor scattered with fallen sycamore, ash, and oak trees. The article notes that while the storms were gentler in this area than elsewhere, they still caused significant damage, with trunks now crisscrossing the ground. Among the casualties are several ash trees, some of which display patterns running through their trunks.

The narrative contrasts these fallen trees with a specific ash tree that appeared highly vulnerable due to ash dieback and a visible split in its trunk. This tree had been monitored by a trail camera set up by the author’s father to capture its potential collapse. Despite its precarious condition and the audibly groaning movement of its split trunk, this particular ash tree survived the two storms that passed through the region. The piece highlights the puzzling disparity between the trees that fell and those, like this specific ash, that remained standing.
summary: Recent storms in Norfolk caused sycamores, ashes, and an oak to fall in a woodland, while a vulnerable ash tree survived. The article examines why some trees fell and others did not, noting that fallen trunks reveal a pattern known as spalting.
author: Guardian Environment

title: El Niño to Raise Childbirth Mortality Risk for Millions, Warn Midwives
content:
Midwives have warned that El Niño will significantly increase the risk of maternal death in the world’s harshest crisis zones. The extreme weather patterns associated with this phenomenon are expected to peak in the coming months, posing a particular threat to pregnant women in countries that already experience high rates of maternal and newborn deaths.

The convergence of floods, cyclones, and extreme heat is forecast to be fatal for many. A primary concern is that these severe weather events may cut off access to hospitals for women in labor, leaving them without necessary medical care during critical moments of childbirth.
summary: Midwives warn that El Niño will raise the risk of death in childbirth for millions of women in crisis zones. Floods, cyclones and extreme heat are expected to peak in coming months, cutting pregnant women off from hospitals during labor.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Johns Hopkins, Academia Sinica Develop RNA Therapy for Brain Receptor Disorders
content: Scientists at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine and Academia Sinica in Taiwan have developed an experimental RNA-based treatment. In mice carrying a rare genetic mutation associated with autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disability, the therapy prevents brain damage and improves learning, memory, and social behavior.
summary: Researchers at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine and Academia Sinica developed an experimental RNA-based treatment targeting a rare genetic mutation. The therapy prevents brain damage and improves learning, memory, and social behavior in affected mice.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Researchers block scar‑forming protein to prevent severe heart failure in mice
content: Researchers have successfully prevented severe heart failure in a mouse model of heart attack by blocking a protein that triggers excessive scar tissue formation. This development addresses a major cause of heart failure, which is currently characterized by a buildup of excess scar tissue in the heart that lacks available treatments.
summary: Researchers prevented severe heart failure in a mouse model of heart attack by blocking a protein that triggers excessive scar tissue formation. This addresses the lack of current treatments for scar buildup that causes most heart failure cases.
author: Medical Xpress

title: US congenital syphilis rates rose sixfold from 2012 to 2022
content: A new study published in Clinical Infectious Diseases reports that congenital syphilis rates among U.S. newborns increased nearly sixfold between 2012 and 2022. The data indicate rising rates across all demographics and income levels, with the sharpest increases observed among Native Americans.
summary: A study in Clinical Infectious Diseases reports that congenital syphilis rates among US newborns increased nearly sixfold between 2012 and 2022. The data indicate rising rates across all demographics and income levels, with the sharpest increases observed among Native Americans.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Drug safety info must remain accessible as patients shift from websites to AI
content: As patients increasingly rely on AI systems to find medication answers, often bypassing original sources, the accessibility of drug safety information becomes critical. Experts emphasize that the utility of prescription drug warnings depends not only on their accuracy but also on how and where individuals receive this data.
summary: Prescription drug warnings can be accurate yet difficult for patients to use, making the delivery method crucial. This is increasingly important as patients rely on AI systems for medication answers without visiting original sources.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Final trial results show promising long-term survival with lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab in advanced thymic tumors
content: Final results from the phase 2 PECATI clinical trial indicate promising long-term survival for patients with previously treated advanced B3-thymoma and thymic carcinoma. The study evaluated the combination therapy of lenvatinib and pembrolizumab, demonstrating encouraging outcomes for this specific patient population.
summary: Final results from the phase 2 PECATI clinical trial demonstrate encouraging long-term survival outcomes with the combination of lenvatinib and pembrolizumab in patients with previously treated advanced B3-thymoma and thymic carcinoma.
author: Medical Xpress

title: AI 'childhood' research offers insights into language development
content: The article suggests that giving AI a “childhood” could illuminate how language develops. It notes that parents observe a baby beginning life without understanding any words, yet over a few years the child learns thousands of words, follows complex sentences, and begins to communicate its own thoughts, a process that scientists still cannot fully explain.
summary: Every parent has watched a baby enter the world unable to understand a single word, yet within a few years it recognizes thousands of words, follows complex sentences, and communicates its own thoughts. The article notes that no scientist can fully explain how this language development occurs.
author: Medical Xpress

title: New study finds early changes in ovarian cancer may leave blood trace
content: A new study suggests that early changes linked to ovarian cancer may leave a trace in the blood. The most common type, high‑grade serous ovarian cancer, grows rapidly and often originates in a fallopian tube, the tube that carries eggs from the ovaries toward the uterus.
summary: A new study suggests that early changes linked to ovarian cancer may leave a trace in the blood. The most common type of ovarian cancer, high‑grade serous ovarian cancer, often starts in the fallopian tube.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Researchers trial AI coach to help manage type 2 diabetes
content:
Researchers are conducting a trial of an artificial‑intelligence coach designed to support people with type 2 diabetes. The study focuses on the difficulty many patients face in maintaining the daily habits required to manage the condition.

The primary challenge is not knowing what actions to take, but consistently following them. Long‑term adherence to healthier eating patterns, regular exercise, and medication regimens is essential for keeping the disease under control.

Because diabetes can progress quietly, missing a dose or skipping exercise may not produce immediate symptoms. This subtle progression, combined with the demands of work, family, and everyday life, can cause healthy intentions to slip, underscoring the need for tools that help sustain consistent self‑management.
summary: Researchers are testing an AI coach to help people with type 2 diabetes maintain healthy eating, exercise, and medication routines. The study notes that diabetes can progress quietly, so missed doses or skipped exercise may not show immediate consequences, making consistency difficult amid daily demands.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Soil Association Withdraws Organic Certification from Salmon After 20 Years
content:
The Soil Association announced this week that it has withdrawn its organic certification for salmon after a 20‑year partnership. The decision follows concerns about environmental and welfare practices that have come to light in the industry.

The first recorded farmed salmon haul in Britain was 14 tonnes off the west coast of Scotland near Fort William in 1971. Unilever, the multinational that pioneered salmon farming, had spent years experimenting with fish cages, disease control, and weather resilience. By the 1960s the company had identified a market opportunity, noting that salmon had previously been a wild catch and a relative luxury. In 1976 Unilever had expanded to three Scottish sites, producing 116 tonnes of fish each year.

The withdrawal marks the end of a long‑standing organic status for British salmon, prompting questions about the sector’s sustainability and animal welfare standards.
summary: The Soil Association withdrew its organic certification from salmon this week, ending a 20‑year partnership. Salmon farming in Britain began in 1971 with a modest 14‑tonne haul off Fort William, and by 1976 Unilever expanded to three Scottish sites producing 116 tonnes each year.
author: Guardian Business

title: Donald Trump Jr leaves paid adviser role at prediction market Kalshi
content: Kalshi announced on Thursday that Donald Trump Jr is no longer a paid adviser for the prediction‑market company. The firm said the change was a mutual business decision between the parties. It followed a decision by Trump Jr’s investment firm, 1789 Capital, to increase its investment in Kalshi’s biggest competitor, Polymarket. Meanwhile, Democrats have said they plan to investigate the Trump family’s investments.
summary: Donald Trump Jr is no longer a paid adviser for Kalshi, the prediction market company announced Thursday. Kalshi said the departure was a mutual business decision that followed 1789 Capital's decision to increase its investment in Polymarket, Kalshi's biggest competitor.
author: Guardian Business

title: Just-in-time supply chains prove risky as pandemic disrupts global manufacturing
content:
Hannah Walker argues that systems built to minimise expenditure in the name of efficiency can become less capable of meeting their intended purpose.  

In a piece by Steven Strogatz and Alex Townsend titled The efficiency trap: why optimising everything can backfire, badly (8 November), the authors warn that excessive optimisation creates hidden risks that extend beyond mathematics and artificial intelligence.  

The widespread adoption of just‑in‑time supply chains illustrates this danger. By eliminating inventories and spare capacity, businesses cut costs and improved efficiency, but those savings shifted risk into invisible vulnerabilities that were revealed when global manufacturing was disrupted during the pandemic.
summary: Hannah Walker argues that systems designed to minimise expenditure for efficiency can become less capable of fulfilling their purpose. The article by Steven Strogatz and Alex Townsend says the widespread adoption of just‑in‑time supply chains eliminated inventories and spare capacity, reducing costs but creating invisible risks that the pandemic‑induced disruption of global manufacturing exposed.
author: Guardian Business

title: Nvidia names CFO Colette Kress interim CEO after Jensen Huang resignation
content:
Nvidia’s leadership is in transition after co‑founder and CEO Jensen Huang resigned amid a series of allegations. Huang’s departure followed claims of multiple extramarital affairs, including one involving an alleged Chinese spy and two with company employees. The company has named its chief financial officer, Colette Kress, as interim CEO on a short‑term basis. Kress reportedly was disparaged by Huang during a summer meeting, yet she will oversee Nvidia while the board searches for a permanent replacement.

The search for a new full‑time CEO is ongoing. While Kress could remain in the role permanently, Nvidia may also consider other candidates. Names that have surfaced include Ian Buck, who manages Nvidia’s AI hardware and software products, and Rene Haas, a former Nvidia employee who is currently the CEO of Arm Holdings, a UK‑based chipmaker. The board’s final decision has yet to be announced.
summary: Jensen Huang resigned amid multiple allegations of extramarital affairs. Nvidia appointed its chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim CEO while it searches for a permanent replacement.
author: Guardian Business

title: Datacenter Industry Uses Propaganda to Suppress Community Opposition
content: Big tech has used misdirection, disinformation and jargon to obscure the harm the facilities can cause to communities “Antifa”. “Commies”. “Chinese bots”. Everyone from tech leaders to the president has called datacenter resistance a “ documented psyop ” and a “ Chinese PR thing ”. But why do they make these claims? Our new research finds that the datacenter industry uses propaganda, disinformation, and information control to mold public opinion and undermine community opposition.
summary: Big tech has used misdirection, disinformation, and jargon to obscure the harm datacenter facilities can cause to communities. New research shows the industry uses propaganda, disinformation, and information control to mold public opinion and undermine community opposition.
author: Guardian Business

title: Trump bought up to $5 million of Nvidia stock before rescinding export rule
content:
President Donald Trump purchased up to $5 million of Nvidia stock before his administration rescinded a Biden‑era export rule. An analysis reports that the stock purchase, worth millions of dollars, occurred as Trump made policy decisions that would benefit the chipmaker.

In May 2025, the Trump administration revoked the rule that had limited Nvidia’s ability to sell the most advanced U.S.–made AI chips to China, removing the restriction on those exports.
summary: Donald Trump purchased up to $5 million of Nvidia stock. In May 2025 his administration rescinded a Biden-era rule that had limited Nvidia’s ability to export advanced AI chips to China.
author: Guardian Business

title: Jaguar Land Rover posts £451m loss after cutting 4,000 jobs
content:
Jaguar Land Rover reported a £451 million loss for the quarter, reflecting the £530 million cost of cutting 4,000 jobs. The British automaker’s revenue rose to £5.9 billion between July and September, but the job reductions were announced near the end of that period amid tough trading conditions.

The company’s chief executive urged the European Union and Britain to cooperate in response to competition from Chinese electric‑car manufacturers.
summary: Jaguar Land Rover reported a £451 million quarterly loss while counting the cost of cutting 4,000 jobs. The company said revenue rose to £5.9 billion for July‑September but costs from the job cuts were £530 million, and its chief executive urged the EU and Britain to cooperate against Chinese electric‑car competition.
author: Guardian Business

title: Water‑activated polymer hardens underwater and bonds glass fragments
content: A water‑activated polymer has been reported that can form solid shapes while submerged and can bond glass fragments. The development addresses the longstanding difficulty of reproducing cement’s hydraulic property in organic polymers, which typically react with moisture but lack the bulk curing and water‑resistance needed for reliable hardening in wet conditions.
summary: A water‑activated polymer can form solid shapes underwater and bond glass fragments. Replicating cement’s hydraulicity in organic polymers has been difficult because moisture‑reactive polymers often lack bulk curing and water resistance needed for reliable wet hardening.
author: Phys.org

title: Ocean carbon uptake rises since 1990 as land uptake stalls, study finds
content: A new study led by scientists at UC San Diego’s Scripps Institution of Oceanography finds that, since 1990, the ocean’s absorption of carbon dioxide from fossil‑fuel emissions has risen steadily. In contrast, the net carbon uptake by forests, soils and other land ecosystems has not increased over the same period.
summary: The ocean has been absorbing carbon dioxide from fossil fuel emissions at an increasing rate since 1990. Net carbon uptake by forests, soils and other land ecosystems has not grown, according to a new study led by scientists at UC San Diego's Scripps Institution of Oceanography.
author: Phys.org

title: Astronomers find red giant with unseen companion, possible supermassive neutron star
content: Astronomers using data from LAMOST and APOGEE have identified a red‑giant star with an unseen binary companion. The companion cannot be seen directly, but its gravitational influence on the giant is measurable. The team describes the object as a likely supermassive neutron star, a candidate that could illuminate the mass gap between typical neutron stars and black holes.
summary: A team of astronomers identified a red giant star with an unseen binary companion using data from LAMOST and APOGEE. The companion cannot be seen directly but its gravitational influence on the red giant suggests it may be a supermassive neutron star that could illuminate the mass gap between neutron stars and black holes.
author: Phys.org

title: Study links two mountain growth spurts to bursts of biological diversity
content: Mountain ranges grew higher throughout Earth's history in two distinct "spurts" that correlated with the flourishing of biological diversity on our planet, according to new research published in the journal Science Advances. The study suggests mountains may have played a key role in sparking complex life.
summary: Mountain ranges grew higher in two distinct spurts throughout Earth's history, according to new research published in Science Advances. The researchers say these spurts coincided with flourishing biological diversity and may have helped spark complex life.
author: Phys.org

title: Evolution discovers new way to build primate brain
content: Scientists are investigating why the human brain is larger and more complex than many other mammals’ brains. Research highlighted in the report focuses on DNA, noting that some genetic changes allow the developing brain to generate more cells, while other findings explain how long those cells can keep multiplying.
summary: Scientists are investigating why the human brain is larger and more complex than many other mammals. Recent findings show genetic changes can increase cell production in the developing brain and extend the period those cells can multiply.
author: Phys.org

title: Study finds social relationships in scaling agricultural innovations are underreported
content: A study in Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems reports that while partnerships and institutional collaboration appear frequently in climate‑oriented agricultural research, their connection to scaling agricultural innovations is seldom documented. The authors argue that clearer insight into social relationships is needed to improve the design, monitoring and evaluation of scaling processes.
summary: A study published in Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems notes that partnerships and institutional collaboration are prominent in climate-oriented agricultural research but are rarely documented in relation to scaling innovations. The findings highlight the need to better understand the role of social relationships to strengthen the design, monitoring and evaluation of scaling processes.
author: Phys.org

title: SpaceX Starship reaches orbit after booster explodes in Gulf of Mexico
content: SpaceX attempted to recover its entire Starship at the launch pad, but the booster fell into the Gulf of Mexico and exploded on Friday, preventing the planned double‑catch recovery. Nevertheless, the Starship vehicle still reached orbit, marking its boldest test to date.
summary: SpaceX's attempt to recover its entire Starship at the launch pad was thwarted when the booster fell into the Gulf of Mexico and exploded on Friday. The Starship still soared into orbit in its boldest test yet.
author: Phys.org

title: New Scientist readers share how the magazine has shaped their lives
content:
New Scientist readers recount how the magazine has shaped their lives

New Scientist celebrated its 70th anniversary by inviting subscribers to share how they first encountered the publication and how it has influenced their personal and professional journeys. The magazine’s first issue appeared on 22 November 1956, and the responses collected from readers of all ages highlighted the breadth of its impact.

Among the stories, one subscriber, who was 13 when he bought the inaugural issue, has remained a subscriber for seven decades. He recalls saving a shilling from Saturday‑morning “jobs” to purchase the first edition and notes that the magazine covered events such as the opening of the Jodrell Bank telescope in 1957. Another reader, who was 12 in 1956, remembers receiving the first copy in a second‑year physics class at Bec Grammar School, describing the paper’s grey pages and the sense that it would follow him throughout life.

Other anecdotes include a student who discovered the magazine in a girls’ grammar school library in the mid‑1960s, who was inspired by an article on Einstein’s relativity and later pursued physical and material sciences before turning to pottery. A group of twelve women meet monthly to discuss New Scientist articles on AI, quantum computing, and climate change, noting the magazine’s role in keeping them engaged with new discoveries.

Several readers also highlighted how specific stories sparked career paths. One individual was motivated by a 2019 article on a microbe’s potential to cause various conditions, leading to a life in life sciences. Another was influenced by a 1980s study on the brain’s decision‑making gap, which informed his work as a psychotherapist. A former engineer recalled a 1959/60 article about dolphins interfering with torpedo tests, which inspired his engineering career.

The collection also features lighter moments, such as a reader who launched a maggot on a 3‑pence firework rocket after reading a New Scientist piece, and a poet who credits the magazine’s writers for inspiring 26 of her children’s science poems. A couple who met on the magazine’s dating site in 2012 celebrated 11 years of marriage, and a reader who has been publishing in the magazine’s “The Last Word” column since 1997 describes the experience as a form of mindfulness.

Overall, the responses underscore New Scientist’s enduring presence in the lives of its readers, shaping careers, hobbies, and conversations across generations.
summary: New Scientist invited subscribers of all ages to recount how they first encountered the magazine and how it has influenced them. The replies featured a range of experiences, from buying the inaugural 1956 issue and conducting a maggot rocket experiment to meeting a spouse via the magazine’s dating site and creating science‑inspired poetry.
author: New Scientist

title: AI system speeds laser simulation up to 250× faster, aiding X‑ray laser research
content:
Researchers at Stanford, UCLA and SLAC have created an AI system that simulates complex laser interactions far faster than conventional methods, with a speed increase described as 250 times in the headline and as thousands of times faster in the report.  

The system can predict how laser pulses behave inside special crystals in just milliseconds while preserving most of the accuracy, a development that could markedly improve the precision and efficiency of powerful X‑ray lasers used in advanced scientific research.
summary: Researchers at Stanford, UCLA and SLAC have created an AI system that simulates complex laser interactions thousands of times faster than conventional methods. The system can predict laser pulse behavior inside special crystals in milliseconds with minimal loss of accuracy, potentially improving the precision and efficiency of powerful X‑ray lasers.
author: Science Daily

title: Scientists observe electrons jumping across forbidden energy gaps in graphene
content: Scientists have observed electrons in graphene making jumps across forbidden energy gaps, a behavior described as seemingly impossible. Some of these transitions occurred with a reported 100 % probability, providing an unprecedented view of quantum dynamics and suggesting potential pathways toward ultrafast, light‑controlled electronic devices.
summary: Scientists captured electrons making seemingly impossible jumps across forbidden energy gaps in graphene, with some transitions occurring at 100% probability. The breakthrough provides an unprecedented view of quantum behavior and may enable a new generation of ultrafast, light-controlled electronics.
author: Science Daily

title: Study finds forced smiles can worsen mood
content: New research indicates that forcing yourself to smile does not always improve mood. In a University of Florida study of more than 1,100 participants, a single artificial smile produced a modest mood lift, but repeatedly faking smiles eliminated that boost and could even worsen feelings.
summary: Researchers at the University of Florida studied more than 1,100 people and found that a single artificial smile can give a small mood boost. Repeatedly faking smiles, however, can erase that benefit or even reverse it, making people feel worse.
author: Science Daily

title: Scientists find evidence of deliberate killings in 5,000-year-old Egyptian king skulls
content: Scientists reexamining 46 ancient skulls from the tombs of Egypt’s first kings have uncovered evidence of potentially fatal head injuries in 18 of the specimens. The study suggests that at least 39% of those examined may have been deliberately killed. These findings lend support to a century‑old theory that royal attendants were sacrificed when kings died, possibly to serve them in the afterlife.
summary: Scientists reexamining 46 ancient skulls found potentially fatal head injuries on 18, indicating that at least 39% of those studied may have been deliberately killed. The findings support a century-old theory that royal attendants were sacrificed when kings died to serve them in the afterlife.
author: Science Daily

title: Yale researchers find drugs, diet, exercise slow aging; supplements ineffective
content:
Yale researchers have found that certain prescription drugs, healthy diets, and exercise can measurably slow biological aging. In contrast, popular anti‑aging supplements appear largely ineffective.

Their analysis of 51 studies could transform how scientists evaluate anti‑aging treatments, though it remains unclear whether these biological changes actually extend life.
summary: Yale researchers have discovered that certain prescription drugs, healthy diets, and exercise can measurably slow biological aging, while popular anti-aging supplements appear largely ineffective. Their analysis of 51 studies could transform how scientists evaluate anti-aging treatments, although whether these biological changes actually extend life remains uncertain.
author: Science Daily

title: Video: New alternative to BMI could stop millions of obesity misdiagnoses
content: An alternative to BMI for diagnosing obesity could prevent misdiagnosis in millions worldwide, doctors report, noting the new method more accurately separates healthy individuals from those with harmful excess body fat. In the Guardian Science video, editor Ian Sample co‑hosts Madeleine Finlay to explain why BMI is flawed and how the new framework could enhance precision medicine.
summary: Doctors say an alternative to BMI could prevent misdiagnosis in millions worldwide by more accurately distinguishing healthy people from those with harmful excess body fat. Guardian Science editor Ian Sample and co‑host Madeleine Finlay discuss why BMI is flawed and how the new framework could improve precision medicine.
author: Guardian Science

title: FAA nationwide ground stop ends after five-hour ordeal
content: The FAA nationwide ground stop concluded Friday evening after a five‑hour pause. Flights will resume, but the effects of the stoppage are expected to be felt throughout the weekend.
summary: The five-hour ordeal ended Friday evening. Planes will be allowed to fly again, but the effects of the stoppage will be felt throughout the weekend.
author: Wired

title: US Transport Secretary says old ATC system caused ground stop, delays persist
content: Passengers are still encountering delays and cancellations even after the United States lifted the nationwide ground stop. U.S. Transport Secretary Sean Duffy said the stoppage resulted from an “incredibly old” air‑traffic‑control system and cautioned that restoring normal operations will take time.
summary: Passengers continue to face delays and cancellations after the nationwide ground stop was lifted. US Transport Secretary Sean Duffy blamed the stoppage on an "incredibly old" air traffic control system and warned that it will take time for normal operations to resume.
author: Euronews

title: Russia urges IIHF to move Canada World Juniors as hockey boycotts spread
content: Russia has urged the International Ice Hockey Federation to relocate the World Junior Championship being held in Canada. Canadian authorities said Russian players will be barred from the 10‑nation tournament in Alberta beginning 26 December. Estonia, Finland and Norway have announced plans to exclude athletes until the war in Ukraine ends.
summary: Canadian authorities announced that Russian players will be barred from the 10‑nation tournament in Alberta starting 26 December. Estonia, Finland and Norway plan to exclude athletes until the war in Ukraine ends.
author: Euronews

title: France asks EU Commission to examine Algeria's non‑compliance with EU association agreement
content: France said on Friday it will request that the European Commission examine Algeria’s alleged breach of its EU association agreement. The move follows Algeria’s near‑blanket ban on French imports announced in July and a suspension of urea shipments to France last month.
summary: France said on Friday it will request the European Commission to examine Algeria's non‑compliance with its EU association agreement. Algeria previously imposed a near‑blanket ban on French imports in July and suspended urea shipments to France last month.
author: France 24

title: US flights resume Saturday after longest nationwide ground stop, 2,000+ still canceled
content:
Flights in the United States began resuming on Saturday after the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years. While airlines work to restore normal schedules, more than 2,000 flights have been cancelled since operations restarted.

The previous day, Friday, saw nearly 6,000 cancellations. The grounding event was only the second time an alert to halt all flights has been issued in U.S. airspace since the September 11 attacks.
summary: Flights in the United States began resuming on Saturday after the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years. More than 2,000 flights remain canceled, following nearly 6,000 cancellations on Friday, the second all‑flight ground alert since the 9/11 attacks.
author: France 24

title: US flights resume after nationwide ground stop lifted, Duffy cites old hardware
content: The United States on Friday lifted an hours-long ground stop at the nation's airports, with top officials explaining that the disruption was not due to a cyberattack or a sweeping Microsoft outage. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that US airspace was now "opened up," and blamed "old hardware" for the travel chaos.
summary: The United States lifted an hours-long ground stop at the nation's airports on Friday. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said US airspace was opened up, blamed old hardware for the disruption, and said it was not due to a cyberattack or a Microsoft outage.
author: France 24

title: FAA lifts nationwide ground stop on all US flights
content: On Friday, the United States lifted an hours‑long nationwide ground stop that had halted flights at airports across the country. Federal Aviation Administration officials clarified that the disruption was not caused by a cyberattack or a broad Microsoft outage.
summary: The United States on Friday lifted an hours-long ground stop at the nation's airports. Top officials said the disruption was not due to a cyberattack or a sweeping Microsoft outage.
author: France 24

title: Microsoft says all services fully recovered after global outage
content: Microsoft confirmed on Saturday morning that its services—including Teams, Outlook, Copilot and other applications—have fully recovered, ending a global outage that disrupted online communications for businesses and governments for more than 24 hours. The U.S. homeland security chief later stated there was “no Microsoft link” to the recent U.S. air stoppage.
summary: Microsoft confirmed on Saturday morning that all services across Teams, Outlook, Copilot and other applications have recovered, ending a global outage that disrupted online communications for businesses and governments for more than 24 hours. The US homeland security chief said there was no Microsoft link to the US air stoppage.
author: France 24

title: France prepares 70,000 police for fifth wave of student protests
content: France expects 50 to 60 student marches on Saturday, with Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez planning to deploy roughly 70,000 police officers and gendarmes nationwide. In Paris, the demonstration is scheduled to begin at 1 p.m., moving from Place de la République toward Place de la Nation via Bastille.
summary: Between 50 and 60 marches are expected in France on Saturday, according to Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez, who plans to mobilise approximately 70,000 police officers and gendarmes across the country. In Paris, the march will commence at 1pm from Place de la République heading towards Place de la Nation via Bastille.
author: France 24

title: SpaceX Starship launch sees booster explode over Gulf of Mexico
content: SpaceX launched its largest rocket, aiming to catch and later reuse both stages for the first time. During the flight, the booster detonated over the Gulf of Mexico, while the spacecraft portion proceeded into orbit.
summary: SpaceX launched its Starship rocket and aimed to catch and reuse both stages. The booster exploded over the Gulf of Mexico while the spacecraft continued into orbit.
author: DW World

title: Gen Z protests raise question if Baby Boomers had better prospects in Germany
content: DW examined data on generational outlooks in Germany, asking whether today’s young people should be more concerned about their future than Baby Boomers were in the 1980s and 1990s and whether both cohorts might join protests together. The piece frames the issue as a comparison of worries across generations.
summary: DW examined data to compare concerns of German young people with those of Baby Boomers in the 1980s and 1990s. The article asks whether both generations should take to the streets and protest together.
author: DW World

title: Istanbul arrest of German foundation employee underscores Erdogan pressure tactics
content: An employee of a German foundation was arrested in Istanbul this week, drawing renewed attention to pressure tactics attributed to the Erdogan administration. Officials note that this detention is not the first similar case involving critics of the Turkish government.
summary: An employee of a German foundation was arrested in Istanbul this week, drawing attention to the Erdogan administration's pressure tactics. The arrest is not the first such case.
author: DW World

title: Nigeria's 2027 polls face AI-driven disinformation concerns
content: Nigeria is approaching its 2027 elections, and the deployment of artificial intelligence within the electoral process has sparked concerns about the integrity of the vote and the readiness of institutions to manage it. Observers are questioning whether Nigerians can trust their democratic processes amid the rise of AI‑driven disinformation.
summary: Nigeria is moving toward its 2027 polls as artificial intelligence is being used in the electoral process. The AI involvement has sparked questions about election integrity, institutional readiness, and whether Nigerians can trust their democratic processes.

title: Astronaut Suni Williams rides through NYC as Grand Marshal of the Veterans Day Parade | Space photo of the day for Nov. 13, 2026
content: NASA astronaut Suni Williams rides through New York City as the Grand Marshal of the Veterans Day Parade on Nov. 11, 2026. (Image credit: Photo by Slaven Vlasic/Getty Images) New Yorkers got a space-y surprise on Wednesday (Nov. 11): Retired NASA astronaut and U. S. This year, the parade featured Suni Williams as its grand marshal. "I’m proud to join New Yorkers and Americans from around the country in honoring the service, sacrifice, and commitment of veterans from every generation," she said during the event. Why is it incredible? Williams was selected for NASA's astronaut program in 1998 and retired from it in December 2025. She spent 608 days in space during her astronaut career, the second-most by an American astronaut behind Peggy Whitson, who racked up 695. Williams also had an extensive career in the U. S. Navy. She began as an ensign in 1987 before serving in a number of different roles. For example, she was a diving officer and a naval aviator and also provided helicopter combat support during Operation Desert Shield and Operation Provide Comfort. She further served as a squadron safety officer and finally as a captain, a rank she achieved in 2017. During this time, Williams supported relief efforts following Hurricane Andrew, trained within the U. S. Naval Test Pilot School and gained a wealth of further experience flying as a military pilot. Williams is part of a longstanding tradition of astronauts serving in the U. S. Military. From test pilots to naval officers and more, there's a strong link between the U. S. Armed forces and NASA's astronaut program.

title: Mariner 9 becomes first spacecraft to orbit Mars on Nov. 13, 1971
content:
On November 13, 1971, NASA’s Mariner 9 became the first spacecraft to enter orbit around Mars. At the time of the launch, scientists had only limited knowledge of the Red Planet. Earlier Mars fly‑bys had revealed a cratered surface, leading some to think Mars resembled the Moon. Mariner 9 changed that perception when it arrived in the middle of a global dust storm. The probe’s cameras captured tall structures that, once the dust settled, were identified as the tops of huge volcanoes. Among them was Olympus Mons, the tallest volcano in the solar system.

The mission also revealed Valles Marineris, an enormous canyon five times longer than the Grand Canyon in Arizona. Mariner 9 mapped 85 % of the planet’s surface during its nearly one‑year orbit. It carried four primary instruments—a camera system, an ultraviolet spectrometer, an infrared spectrometer, and an infrared radiometer—that enabled the discovery of 20 giant volcanoes and detailed mapping of Valles Marineris, which stretches 2,500 miles (4,000 km) long and 120 miles (200 km) wide. The canyon was named in honor of the spacecraft.

In total, Mariner 9 took 7,329 photographs of Mars, achieving a resolution of between ½ and 1 mile (1–2 km). It also captured at least 80 images of Mars’ two small moons, Phobos and Deimos. The probe’s gaseous nitrogen supply, used to feed its attitude‑control thrusters, ran dry by February 1972. NASA shut the mission down in October 1972 after the spacecraft had completed its orbit.

Mariner 9’s achievements cemented its place in space history. It was the first human‑made object to orbit Mars, beating the Soviet Union’s Mars 2 spacecraft to the planet despite Mars 2’s 11‑day head start. The data gathered by Mariner 9 transformed the image of Mars from a mysterious, moon‑like world into a fully mapped planet, laying the groundwork for future exploration.
summary: On Nov. 13, 1971, NASA's Mariner 9 entered orbit around Mars, the first human‑built craft to do so. The mission mapped about 85% of the planet, revealing features such as Olympus Mons and the Valles Marineris canyon.

title: Millions of Americans are not taking their GLP-1 drugs as prescribed
content:
GLP‑1 medications have become widely used for diabetes, weight loss, and several other chronic conditions, including cardiovascular disease and obstructive sleep apnea. A new study from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) shows that the drugs are also being used in ways that diverge from medical prescriptions.

The CDC researchers analyzed survey data collected in July and August 2025 from more than 8,000 U.S. adults. Their estimates indicate that about 9.8 percent of U.S. adults—roughly 27 million people—used a glucagon‑like peptide‑1 receptor agonist in 2025. The study was published in the CDC’s Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report.

Among those who reported using a GLP‑1 drug, 44 percent said they altered their use from the prescribed regimen. Reported changes included skipping doses, delaying refills, and taking smaller doses, among other modifications.

More than half of the users who changed their usage cited cost or availability as the reason for doing so. Cost and access barriers were most pronounced among younger adults: 58 percent of users aged 14‑39 who modified their use named cost as a barrier, compared with only 20 percent of users aged 65 or older who reported the same.
summary: GLP-1 medications are everywhere these days. The peptide-based drugs are both highly effective and wildly popular for diabetes, weight loss and a growing range of connected chronic health conditions, including cardiovascular disease and obstructive sleep apnea.

title: California's brand-new Air & Space Center, home of the space shuttle Endeavour, opens today
content:
The California Science Center in Los Angeles officially opened its new Samuel Oschin Air & Space Center to the public on November 13. This massive new wing, which has been in development for more than three decades, centers on the retired space shuttle Endeavour. The spacecraft is displayed upright in its launch position, standing nearly 200 feet tall. Former NASA astronaut Garrett Reisman, who flew on two space shuttle missions including one on Endeavour, described the initial reveal of the shuttle as an overwhelming experience. He noted that the exhibit provides a significant opportunity for people from around the world to visit Los Angeles and see the shuttle, creating a "force multiplier" for exposing children and families to space exploration.

Visitors enter the exhibit through a video presentation that culminates in a dramatic unveiling of the shuttle, which completed 25 missions to Earth orbit between 1992 and 2011. The display features a replica launch tower that allows guests to look down at the spacecraft. At the base of the shuttle, there are numerous interactive exhibits, including a shuttle landing simulator, a replica cockpit, and various space artifacts from decades of spaceflight history. While visitors can use elevators or stairs to navigate the space, they can also slide down to the base of the exhibit.

The interior of the shuttle is open for inspection, allowing visitors to peer inside at the robotic arm, handles, straps, and electronic gear. The exhibit is designed for all ages and offers multiple vantage points, including a view from underneath the engines and a transparent floor at the top of the launch tower that allows visitors to stand above the shuttle. Reisman reflected on his time aboard the shuttle, pointing out specific handrails he held during a spacewalk. He explained that seeing these same handrails from the elevator triggers memories of his training and mission, emphasizing the direct connection between the historical artifact and the public experience.

The new air and space center is free to the public, just like the rest of the museum. However, due to the high anticipation surrounding the opening, visitors are required to make online reservations to attend. While the admission is free, there is a cost associated with reserving slots during the busy initial days. The California Science Center encourages visitors to budget a significant amount of time to explore the full range of exhibits and interactive elements available in the new wing.
summary: California's brand-new Air & Space Center, home of the space shuttle Endeavour, opens today.
author: Space.com

title: Rocket Lab launching 100th space mission early on Nov. 14: Watch it live
content:
Rocket Lab is scheduled to launch its 100th space mission, designated "The Mountain God Rises," early Saturday morning, November 14. The Electron rocket, carrying a private Japanese Earth-observing satellite, will lift off from the company’s New Zealand site during a window opening at 12:30 a.m. EST (0530 GMT; 6:30 p.m. local time). Live coverage will begin approximately 30 minutes before launch and is available via Rocket Lab, with Space.com expected to carry the feed.

This milestone marks the 100th launch for the California-based company since its first test flight in May 2017. Although that initial effort failed, the 59-foot-tall Electron rocket successfully delivered cubesats to low Earth orbit in January 2018. Rocket Lab founder and CEO Peter Beck stated during a November 9 earnings call that no commercially developed rocket has reached the 100-launch mark faster, including SpaceX’s Falcon 9. Beck highlighted that the company has achieved a 96% reliability rate across its previous 99 launches, describing the achievement as an unprecedented milestone for a commercial small-lift orbital rocket.

For this specific mission, the Electron rocket features special black livery to commemorate the golden milestone. The launch will be the 11th for Tokyo-based customer iQPS, which is developing a constellation of 36 synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellites. If successful, the rocket’s upper kick stage will deploy a single iQPS spacecraft into an orbit 357 miles (575 kilometers) above Earth. These SAR satellites are capable of imaging the planet through cloud cover and at night, providing advantages over optical-wavelength spacecraft. It is noted that not all of Rocket Lab’s missions are orbital; its suborbital HASTE variant has conducted nine missions to date.
summary: Rocket Lab will launch its 100th space mission early Saturday morning (Nov. 14), and you can watch the milestone liftoff live.

title: The Guardian view on M John Harrison’s Booker win: a new frontier for science fiction | Editorial
content: The End of Everything is a novel for our age of permacrisis. Genre boundaries belong to the past “Science fiction will never be Literature with a capital ‘L,’” began a New York Times review of Margaret Atwood’s novel Oryx and Crake back in 2003. Now, the seemingly impossible has happened – M John Harrison’s The End of Everything is the first science fiction novel to win the Booker prize. Fans have hailed this as a victory for a long-marginalised genre. The author himself was not so sure. “Writing science fiction is the last thing I want to do,” he said with characteristic iconoclasm at an event before the prize. The sci-fi v literary or “mainstream” fiction debate is as endless and battle-strewn as a fantasy saga. The late Ursula K Le Guin, a giant of the form, famously took Atwood to task for her reluctance to use the term science fiction for some of her novels, including Oryx and Crake: “She doesn’t want the literary bigots to shove her into the literary ghetto.” Harrison doesn’t want to break out of the ghetto; he wants to break it down. “I really hate categories, and I really hate being categorised,” he said.
summary: The End of Everything is a novel for our age of permacrisis. Genre boundaries belong to the past “Science fiction will never be Literature with a capital ‘L,’” began a New York Times review of Margaret Atwood’s novel Oryx and Crake back in 2003.

title: Gemini Astronaut Photos Inspired Early Earth Observation Program
content:
NASA astronauts James A. Lovell Jr. and Edwin E. “Buzz” Aldrin Jr. captured images of the Red Sea and Nile river valley on November 14, 1966, during their four-day mission aboard Gemini XII. This flight, which ran from November 11 to 15, marked the final mission of NASA’s Gemini program. While the crew successfully completed rendezvous maneuvers and spacewalks, procedures essential for future Moon missions, they also contributed to the development of Earth observation from space.

The orbital imagery captured by Lovell, Aldrin, and other Gemini astronauts demonstrated the value of such photography for studying Earth’s surface. These images helped scientists build a case for a dedicated Earth observation satellite program. William T. Pecora, the director of the United States Geological Survey from 1965 to 1971, was a key advocate for accelerating the use of these satellites. In a 1969 statement, Pecora noted that the Earth Resources Observation Satellite (EROS) program, which he championed, was conceived in 1966 largely as a direct result of the demonstrated utility of Mercury and Gemini orbital photography for Earth resource studies.

The EROS program later paved the way for Landsat, which has provided invaluable data for over five decades. Today, Landsat and other Earth-observing satellites are used globally to monitor crops, wildfires, flooding, vegetation health, land use, and various other changes to the planet.
summary: Gemini Astronaut Photos Inspired Early Earth Observation Program.

title: It's the end of the world as we know it, per a physicist's 1960 prediction
content: As of this morning, Microsoft is still scrambling to restore service following yesterday's global outage, with millions of users unable to access Outlook and other vital tools. It's not the end of the world, but it does seem fitting that this should happen on the day a physicist predicted would be the end of humanity: November 13, 2026. And it falls on a Friday, too. The physicist in question is Heinz von Foerster, who published a 1960 paper in the journal Science predicting that by today, overpopulation would reach the breaking point. It's not a new fear. English economist Thomas Malthus —one of the early pioneers in modeling population dynamics—made a similar prediction in 1798, claiming that a rapidly growing population would eventually exhaust the available food supply, and humanity would starve to death. His model rested on the assumption of exponential growth, but the equation is only applicable under specific conditions, such as scientists growing bacteria in a lab in a perfectly controlled environment. Even then, while growth occurs exponentially for a time, it does not continue forever. Population dynamics are notoriously tricky to calculate because there are so many variables to consider and so much unpredictability in the system. In his 1960 analysis, Von Foerster accurately measured past trends in population growth, but like Malthus, he assumed those trends would carry into the future largely unchanged. So he projected that human population growth would march inexorably toward infinity. We wouldn't starve to death; von Foerster thought we would be ingenious enough to solve the food supply problem. Instead, "they will be squeezed to death," he wrote. Read full article Comments
summary: It's the end of the world as we know it, per a physicist's 1960 prediction.

title: Nightmare Eclipse releases SignDrop Windows zero‑day giving local users System rights
content:
Nightmare Eclipse, a researcher who has publicly criticized Microsoft, released a new Windows zero‑day on Tuesday. The vulnerability, dubbed SignDrop, allows local users to gain full System rights on certain Windows versions. It is located in the Common Log File System (CLFS), which Microsoft defines as a “general‑purpose logging service used by software clients running in user‑mode or kernel‑mode.”

SignDrop works by forcing a privileged process—such as Windows Defender—to open a specially crafted CLFS container. An attacker with ordinary user privileges can then exploit the privileged file‑creation capability to elevate their rights to System. The attack leverages the interaction between CLFS, Windows Defender, and Windows file permissions. Specifically, it uses the legitimate Defender function ServerMpUpdateEngineSignature, which processes antivirus signature updates, to open the malicious log file.
summary: Nightmare Eclipse, a researcher with a public dispute with Microsoft, disclosed the SignDrop vulnerability that allows local users to gain full System rights on some Windows versions. The flaw lies in the Common Log File System and exploits Windows Defender's privileged file creation to elevate privileges.

title: OpenAI Board Member Warns AI Takeover Could Happen in Months

Speaking at a lecture series this week, Cristiano bluntly told the audience in a Toronto Convention Center, "I think for most people in this room, the most likely reason they will die is because of an AI accident." In the opening lecture of a three-part series, Cristiano outlined his worries about the risk of an impending "AI takeover." He defined that as a situation where goal-pursuing AI systems "call the shots in the same sense that humans today call the shots and what happens on Earth" and where any human trying to stop them "would be as ineffective as if you or me was trying to stop the US military." Such a situation would likely lead to mass death and perhaps uninhabitable environments for humans, Cristiano said. Read full article Comments

content:

Pothier highlighted that Europe’s computing capacity represents only about 5 % of the global total. He noted that, despite a wealth of researchers and expertise, the continent struggles to translate these assets into real technological and industrial scale.

Gödel’s two incompleteness theorems, published in 1931, revolutionised mathematics and paved the way for the digital age. After these seminal results of the 1930s, he published only a few papers. His unpublished work, however, runs to tens of thousands of pages and remains of great interest to historians of science.

title: Snoh Aalegra's 'Legendary Love' review: raw R&B talent restrained by reverence for the greats
content: (Stem) Her truly remarkable, Sade-ish voice is hypnotic against some dizzyingly plush production, but a modern spin on 80s pastiche sometimes veers too close to tribute Swedish-Iranian singer Snoh Aalegra has previously described her music – a lush, pastiche-y mix of R&B, hip-hop, soul and pop – as “cinematic soul”. But although she’s a dab hand at graceful, timeless presentation (and has a truly remarkable voice) Aalegra’s music has often struggled to match up to its aesthetic, hampered by her love of the greats and a penchant for broadly generic lyrics. Her most recent album, 2021’s Temporary Highs in the Violet Skies, made some headway toward carving out a more distinctive sound, thanks to sparky and inventive production from Tyler, the Creator, No ID, P2J and the Neptunes, but still didn’t quite feel like the right fit. Aalegra’s fourth album is her most successful front-to-back statement yet, even if she can’t shake off the talent-show-ish reverence for her idols. Sparse and warm, Legendary Love puts her androgynous, Sade-ish voice in dizzyingly plush environments: a hybrid of Afrobeats and 80s R&B on the hypnotic I Love You ; a bed of minimalist guitars and moonlit synths on This That, which sounds as though it could have been produced by Jai Paul.
summary: The review describes Snoh Aalegra's fourth album, 'Legendary Love', as her most successful front-to-back statement yet, featuring sparse and warm production. Despite her remarkable voice, the album is noted for being hampered by a talent-show-ish reverence for her idols and a modern spin on 80s pastiche.

title: Heartland Review: Jessica Chastain's Netflix Thriller Fails to Hit
content: The Oscar winner plays a singer turned detective searching for her niece in an overly generic Nashville-based mystery that fails to find its footing Given the popularity of its music and the streaming services’ interest in faith-based programming, I’m always a little surprised that there aren’t more movies and TV shows about Nashville. Well, at least the idea of Nashville, the country music mecca that is perpetually struggling to define itself within and against the country at large, a place that has always been more diverse than its reputation yet still stands for a certain image of white, Christian Americana. There are plenty of enduring contradictions to mine there – the hyper-masculine men singing with their hearts on their sleeve, the Madonna-badass complex among its relatively few female stars, the suburban money in a genre ostensibly speaking to the rural common man. Netflix seems to be aiming for some of those complexities with Heartland, a patchy neo-noir thriller starring Jessica Chastain as a washed-up former star turned vigilante detective with an axe to grind on Music Row. Chastain’s Misty Jones is certainly a thorny Nashville archetype, a female lead we might call “unlikable” painted in the stark terms of a bad country song (said with love as someone raised on country radio). The first five minutes of the nearly two-hour feature from Shana Feste, the writer-director perhaps best known for the 2010 movie Country Strong that launched Gwyneth Paltrow’s brief singing career, churn through the greatest hits of on-screen female fuck-up: teary loneliness, near-wordless pick-up of a stranger from the bar, beer bottle on the nightstand, joint in the bathroom, haunting echoes of erstwhile better days (in this case, a Grammy in an empty fridge, which does feel inspired in its bluntness).
summary: Jessica Chastain, an Oscar winner, stars in Netflix's Heartland as a former singer turned detective searching for her niece in a generic Nashville mystery. The film is called a patchy neo-noir thriller that fails to find its footing.

title: Revived art prize gives football its creative due once more
content:
Football and the art world have historically maintained a distance, with the sport being a rare subject for artists in its early decades. Notable exceptions include Umberto Boccioni’s 1913 painting Dynamism of a Soccer Player, Kazimir Malevich’s Painterly Realism of a Football Player – Color Masses in the 4th Dimension, and a smoggy scene titled Any Wintry Afternoon in England currently displayed at the Manchester Art Gallery. These works remained isolated instances of football appearing in fine art.

In 1953, the Football Association launched an art prize supported by the newly formed Arts Council. The winning works included L.S. Lowry’s Going To The Match, which depicts crowds heading to Bolton Wanderers’ then-home ground, Burnden Park. An exhibition of the submissions, titled Football and The Fine Arts, toured the country. The FA secretary, Sir Stanley Rous, expressed hope that the initiative would finally break the barrier between football and the art world. This year’s award entries indicate a healthy revival of this creative intersection.
summary: The breadth of entries for this year's award reveals a healthy revival in the relationship between football and the art world. The Football Association launched an art prize in 1953, backed by the newly formed Arts Council, to break the barrier between those two worlds.

title: Debutant Mahli Beardman takes six wickets as Australia beats England in ODI
content: A week of watching Australian cricket descend into civil war ended with smiles being wiped from English faces after a stunning debut from fast bowler Mahli Beardman consigned the tourists to an all-too-familiar hammering in Perth. Victory in a low-key one-day international was never going to atone for the galling start to that failed Ashes campaign here 12 months ago. Nevertheless, England appeared better prepared this time, while the hosts were missing their big three quicks and fighting sandpaper-related bushfires off the field. And yet by 4.38pm local time – nine hours after Pat Cummins had finished his marathon takedown of Usman Khawaja’s autobiography in Sydney – Harry Brook’s side were 1-0 down once again. Rolled for 131 all out in just 33.4 overs, having been 68 for eight at one stage, a seven-wicket loss was the upshot. There was more than a touch of Cummins about their tormentor on the day, too, with Beardman claiming figures of six for 24 from 7.4 overs in his first ODI – a new national record, no less. Just 21 years old, but already touching 90mph on the speed gun, the Western Australian looks a considerable prospect. Much like Cummins, Beardman has been mentored by the great Dennis Lillee and endured battles with a rebellious body along the way. Even with a first-class debut still pending, it would not be a shock to see him handed a baggy green cap in the coming months or travel to England for the Ashes next year.
summary: Twenty-one-year-old Australian fast bowler Mahli Beardman took a career-best six for 24 in his first ODI to lead Australia to a seven-wicket victory over England in Perth. England was bowled out for 131 all out in 33.4 overs, suffering a defeat that left them trailing 1-0 in the series.

title: MIT study finds sleep CSF waste‑clearing waves impaired in older adults
content:
MIT researchers have identified a decline in a brain‑cleansing process that occurs during sleep in older adults. The study, published today in Nature Aging, shows that waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) that help flush waste from the brain are markedly reduced in people aged 60 to 84 compared with younger adults. The impairment is linked to a decrease in the slow brain waves that normally dominate deep, non‑REM sleep, and the researchers emphasize that it is not simply a consequence of shorter sleep duration.

The investigation recruited two age groups—18 to 39 and 60 to 84—and conducted two‑hour overnight scans that began late at night to encourage sleep. Participants underwent functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), a modified MRI technique developed by senior author Laura Lewis to measure CSF flow, and electroencephalography (EEG) to monitor brain activity. Many subjects fell asleep in the scanner, allowing the team to compare awake and sleeping states. In the younger cohort, the EEG slow waves intensified during non‑REM sleep and the accompanying CSF waves enlarged. In contrast, older participants exhibited CSF waves that were significantly smaller than those seen in the younger group.

To probe the mechanisms behind the age‑related decline, the researchers performed additional awake‑state experiments. They assessed neurovascular coupling by presenting a flickering checkerboard, a stimulus that normally increases neural activity and blood flow. While older subjects showed neural activation, their blood flow response was blunted, indicating diminished vascular responsiveness. A breath‑hold challenge further revealed that older participants had a smaller increase in cerebral blood flow than younger subjects. These two factors explained much, but not all, of the reduced CSF flow, suggesting other age‑related contributors.

The study also noted that some older adults displayed gray‑matter atrophy, which correlated with a greater decrease in CSF flow. While none of the participants had a diagnosed neurodegenerative disorder, the researchers plan to follow individuals longitudinally to determine whether altered CSF dynamics predict future risk. They are also exploring interventions, such as brief bursts of pink noise during sleep, that previously increased CSF flow in younger adults, and aim to test whether such approaches could benefit older participants.

The research was funded by the National Institutes of Health, the Simons Collaboration on Plasticity in the Aging Brain, a McKnight Scholar Award, a Pew Biomedical Scholar Award, an MIT EECS Transformative Research Award, the Picower Institute Neurological Disorder Discovery Research Fund, a Sloan Fellowship, and the Department of Defense National Defense Science and Engineering Graduate Fellowship Program. The lead authors are Sydney Bailes, a postdoc in the MIT Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems, and Stephanie Williams, a former visiting student who earned a PhD from Boston University in 2026. Laura Lewis, the Athinoula A. Martinos Associate Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, is the senior author.
summary: As people age, they may sleep for shorter periods and wake up more frequently during the night. In addition to those disruptions, MIT researchers have now discovered that a process responsible for flushing waste from the brain during sleep is commonly impaired in older people.

title: Silicon Valley Misreads Politics; Nvidia Confirms Chip Tracking for Smuggling

Burkhart argues that volunteers, who play a vital role in developing devices that can control robotic limbs, computers, and even speech, should be recognized for their contributions. These guidelines aim to reduce the reliance on non-disclosure agreements and ensure that participants retain control over their personal data.
